en: Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth,
speak everything exactly as it was heard and as it was seen, straightforwardly.
Setting aside conjecture and refutation, speak according to what has been seen and heard, as it was not seen [before], in accordance with reality. 8.101
One should treat cowherds, merchants, as well as artisans, actors and bards, servants, and usurers—though they be Brahmins—as one would Śūdras. (8.102)

Artisans (*kāravaḥ*) are craftsmen such as carpenters, blacksmiths, cooks, and the like; *kuśīlavas* are dancers, singers, and so forth; *preṣyas* are those known as slaves who carry out the orders of another for the sake of their livelihood; and *vārdhuṣikas* are those who subsist on interest. Even though these are Brāhmaṇas, according to the context, they are to be regarded like Śūdras in testimony and in oaths, but not in other ritual acts. Just as a Śūdra is not questioned regarding gifts, merit, and the like, and is purified in testimony and in oaths by means of carrying fire and so forth, so too is this [Brāhmaṇa] subject to the same oath. Although the oath was not previously introduced, nevertheless, because it follows immediately after, because it involves a fault, and because of the effort required—since proximity is a cause for connection even when there is effort—and because of the immediate sequence with what is about to be stated, it is the same regarding the oath as it was regarding age. (8.102)
A man who speaks thus regarding matters of dharma, even though he knows otherwise, does not fall from the heavenly world; they call that the speech of the gods. 8.103.

The meaning is that one who knows otherwise but speaks otherwise does not fall from heaven; even by speaking falsely, he is not defiled. Is this always the case? No, he says: "In matters concerning dharma" (*dharmato 'rtheṣu*). That is, in legal proceedings (*artheṣu vyavahāreṣu*) caused by dharma, such as compassion and so forth. He will demonstrate in the following verse how dharma serves as the cause. And this is not stated according to his own arbitrary fancy; rather, the authors of the Smṛtis prior to him also spoke these words. What, then, is the "divine speech"? It is the speech belonging to the gods which declares that in this particular circumstance one should speak untruth; having heard this, Manu and others speak it—this is a specific praise of falsehood.

Others, however, have explained this verse as a supplement to the preceding rule. This [explanation] must apply to Brāhmaṇas who are engaged in questioning cowherds and the like. Otherwise, regarding Brāhmaṇas, there is the injunction: "Speak the truth" (MDh 8.88). How then could these Brāhmaṇas be questioned like Śūdras? Even one who knows the law would not be at fault, because Manu and others speak such words so that they may be treated like Śūdras. And they are authorities on what is dharma and what is adharma. By them, the truth must be spoken; and where it is as prescribed, that alone is dharma, whereas where there is falsehood, the speaking of falsehood itself is dharma. (8.103)

In a case where the death penalty would be incurred for a Śūdra, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Brāhmaṇa upon the statement of the truth, there one must speak a falsehood; for that is superior to the truth. (8.104)

In this context, the prohibition "one shall not speak untruth" is stated here as having a scope that excludes Śūdras and others; it is certainly not the case that speaking untruth is being enjoined. If that were so, the syntactic unity with the prohibition would be subverted.

What, then, is the scriptural mention of the occasion (*nimitta*) here? It is the word "therein" (*tatra*). Since that [word] qualifies the killing, it is not the killing itself [that is the occasion], because it is impossible for that which is non-existent (the killing) to serve as an occasion. Consequently, the sense that follows is: "Once the killing has been performed, one must subsequently speak an untruth regarding it, whether it be true or false. But that is untenable.

Now, it might be argued that while "wherein" (yatra) indicates the subject matter of the legal proceeding, "therein" (tatra) refers back to that very same thing; consequently, for that legal proceeding in which they, having been defeated, become liable to execution, its status as a causal basis (nimittabhāva) would be untenable.

On this point, they say: "In this case, a falsehood is not desired even regarding those deserving of death, because the life of a more wicked person is unfit [to be spared]. However, as for one who does not deserve death—on the grounds that the king, due to some lapse such as a minor offense or a failure like arson, might not execute him out of a slight transgression—this is a logical possibility. Yet, because he is a king, the punishment of anger is unscriptural, and since its measure is not fixed, there is no certainty; thus, it is not logical for that [possibility] to serve as a cause [for telling a lie]. Therefore, it is only right that [the rule] should remain a supplement to the prohibition.

In the Gautama-smṛti, however, there is not even the suspicion of a rule permitting falsehood. Since there is a prohibition such as, "There is no fault in speaking untruth if life depends upon it" (GDh 13.24), and since there would otherwise be the contingency of acting according to one's whim regarding both truth and falsehood, it is logical that one who, while intending to kill by means of truthful speech, resorts to falsehood out of fear of transgressing the prohibition "One must not harm any living beings," acts in this way. Therefore, this [falsehood] has been committed; for if he does not speak when questioned, he does not kill. And how can he be tainted by the fault of harming if he does not actually kill?

Now, if it is argued that even though [the king] possesses independence (*svātantrya*), he nevertheless possesses the status of an *instigating agent* (*prayojakakartṛ*) because he is killed by the king's command, thereby becoming the cause (*hetu*) of that action—this is not so; for not every cause is an instigator. For instance, in the expressions "by wealth, the family [is established]" or "by knowledge, fame [is attained]," knowledge and fame possess the causality of being instigators. Nor is this causal state—which is characterized by the suitability for the production of a worldly result—something entirely different from substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*). Even where an action is heard, as in "cooking with fire," that too is expressed in its accomplished form (*siddharūpa*) by means of *kṛt*-suffixes denoting the state (*bhāva*). Furthermore, this scriptural (*śāstrīya*) instigator of the agent’s activity is a cause distinct from that; it is not the case that the status of being an instigator is defined in this way [as mere causality]. If, first of all, the status of being an instigator were restricted to commanding and requesting in the forms of orders and entreaties, then the derivation of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) would be difficult to justify in cases involving insentient things, such as "he causes the rice to dry in the sun."

But has this not already been answered by the commentators? They argue that the phrase "primary and metaphorical action" applies when there is a metaphorical attribution of agency to a sentient entity, as in "the alms cause him to dwell" (*bhikṣā vāsayati*) or "the cow-dung fire causes him to study" (*kārīṣo 'dhyāpayati*). For in these cases, the assistance is not produced by consciousness; rather, it is because another instigator is certain. Indeed, for the student who performs his study as impelled by the injunction to become a teacher, the cold and other such factors act as obstacles; the cow-dung fire is thus figuratively attributed the status of an instigator. For one is called an "instigator" (*prayojaka*) precisely because of their capacity to impel. And this [capacity] is seen even more clearly in non-sentient things like wind and water with respect to fire and wood. Consequently, in the case of injunctions, instigators, praises, and performers, since there is an absence of actual commanding and so forth, the words would have to be taken in a figurative sense. Alternatively, being an instigator consists in performing actions conducive to the purpose. This is an engagement in activities other than commanding and so forth, which is consistent with the operation of the instigator and is termed "arrangement" (*saṃvidhāna*). For it is in the very act of arranging that one is said to "cause to do. For example, for one who desires to eat, one person brings a vessel while another serves the food. For someone intent on killing, one person hands over a weapon while another inflames his fury by exposing the victim's faults. An instigator characterized in this way—one devoid of the form of a commander yet possessing activity—attains a state of favorability toward the accomplishment of the result for the one being prompted, by engaging in actions conducive to that end. This is the position regarding the instigator.
In this view, the cow-dung fuel and the teacher would both be considered equivalent.

In this context as well, that without whose absence the action does not cease, and for whom the designation of a specific *kāraka* would otherwise not apply, is the primary instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*). Without the student, the *kārīṣa* (cow-dung fire) cannot assume its status as a cause for study; however, even without the teacher, the *kārīṣa* is indeed capable [of being a cause], and thus it is a secondary (*gauṇa*) agent. Furthermore, where the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) or other *kāraka* is certain because a suffix denoting a causal agent (*hetumat-pratyaya*) is observed, there too it is only in a secondary sense. For example, seeing someone who has gone repeatedly to a distant village for even a slight purpose, one says, "The horse causes Devadatta to go. But where neither proximity nor distance, nor the distinction between internal (*antaraṅga*) and external (*bahiraṅga*), is perceived, then all those who contribute to the favorability of that action are instigating agents.

But surely, if there is no internal connection (*antaraṅgayoga*) in the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a *kāraka*, what is the distinction between the cow-dung fire (*kārīṣa*) and the teacher (*upādhyāya*)? That [distinction] belongs solely to the grammatical system (*prakriyā*) of your honorable selves; it does not depend on the actual state of things (*vastu*). And injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*) are based on the actual state of things. This too is recited therein: "The *kārakas* arise from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). This being so, where someone might intend to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of one who is actually a non-agent, there both the injunction and the prohibition regarding the agent-suffix (*kartṛ-pratyaya*) would apply. For example, in the enumeration of sins, it is recited: "The buyer and seller, the preparer and the server" (MDh 5.51). Therefore, that rule of yours intended for the successful description of the linguistic system (*anvākhyāna*) does not override the meaning based on the actual state of things.

For this very reason, the commentators have stated: "If the performance of a capable act were the cause [of killing], then it would follow that even a mere cause [would be the killer]. Consequently, if someone gives food to another and that person dies from gluttony due to overeating, the giver would incur the status of being the killer; yet this is not the case. For by means of another action, that instigator known as "feeding" is determined to be neither the killing itself nor the envy and so forth that might somehow serve as a causal condition (*nimitta*). Or, let it be a causal condition; nevertheless, we maintain that because there is an absence of instigation (*prayojakatva*), there is no agency (*kartṛtva*). However, one must consider this: if someone commits an offense by stealing land, gold, or the like, and that person dies from the resentment caused by that theft, does the thief incur only the fault of the theft, or does he also possess the status of being a causal condition (*nimittibhāva*) for the killing? This is what requires reflection.

What is there to deliberate upon here? Since the relationship between cause and effect is understood through its invariable concomitance, it is not possible for the seizure of land and so forth to have a fixed cause [for its occurrence] in the same way as the striking of a sword or the interruption of a meal.

What kind of restriction (*niyama*) is intended here? If it were the case that some die while others do not, then a non-restriction would become a restriction [due to arbitrariness]. This is because of the difference in the individual natures (*svabhāva*) of persons: the very same medicine is beneficial for one suffering from phlegm (*śleṣman*), yet harmful to another. Furthermore, for all entities (*bhāva*), the manifestation of a different capacity depends upon differences in place, time, nature, and auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). That same characteristic [of a thing], depending on the person’s mental continuum (*vitta-saṃtati*), becomes the cause for cutting off thirst when depending on another living being; likewise, for one who is extremely intolerant and full of resentment, the seizure of property, humiliation, and so forth, lead to death. How could the status of these things as a causal condition (*nimitta-bhāva*) be denied in such cases? However, for one of gentle mind, there is only equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward them. Moreover, regarding those who, overcome by resentment, die by means of fasting, falling into a chasm, consuming poison, and so forth, aiming at the wrongdoer—even in that case, this same principle applies.

But surely, since other well-known causes such as consuming poison are observed there [in cases of death], the offense of seizing land and so forth would not incur the status of being a murderer. If it is argued that, because one who has been provoked to anger by that act proceeds toward the cause of death, there is a causal relationship through a mediated succession (*pāraṃparya*), then in that case, some people might commit suicide out of fear even after receiving wholesome advice; consequently, the advisors would be murderers. Likewise, envious people, withering away through jealousy over the property of others, would attribute the fault to the wealthy. Similarly, others of deluded mind who die following their beloved children or masters would entail the status of being murderers for those beloved ones and others. Furthermore, others of feeble mind might become envious upon seeing a beautiful woman, and with broken hearts and minds devoid of discernment, they would find fault with virtuous women. Thus, this very consequence follows: that the deceased incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*).

This is true, provided there were no distinction between injunction and prohibition. Instruction for one's benefit is enjoined, while the seizing of one's property and so forth is prohibited. As they have said: "If, in some way, a reversal occurs for those engaged in doing a favor, there is no fault in that for them, just as [the effect of] medicinal herbs may vary."

In this regard, it is not only the case that there is no fault when a physician or the like, seeking to benefit a patient, administers medicine that somehow results in the opposite effect; rather, it is said that even for another, such as a cow or other animal, if it is pulled from a great mire by the rescuer’s arm and dies despite the effort exerted, the rescuer is not at fault. This applies everywhere in the same way.

Even if someone burns with envy upon seeing another person engaged in their own duties and possessed of an excellence of wealth and form, there is no transgression of the meaning of the treatise on his part. For it is only when the causal condition (*nimittabhāva*) is certain that it can be the object of a prohibition. Furthermore, regarding mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) residing in other living beings, which undergo change at every moment, it is impossible to determine a specific nature [of the cause], such as "this person is being harmed by this excellence of form. And when a certain object of prohibition is possible, it is not logical for it to have an uncertain object.

In that case, where there might even be an understanding of the cause—due to some reversal of the syllables, emaciation of the body, or similar factors on the part of a person overcome by sophistry—what is the point of associating with one who is prone to such failure, or rather, with one who is a woman who kills men?

This is not so. For such a state of affairs, even if it constitutes a cause (*nimitta*), is not the object of a prohibition, because it would contradict another injunction. Indeed, there exists here an injunction prohibiting sexual misconduct (*vyabhicāra*). Nor can injunctions, which find their scope in an area not already occupied by another injunction, be expected to encroach upon the domain of a contradictory injunction. As for those who think that the instruction on the preservation of moral conduct prohibits activity characterized by passion (*rāga*) but not that characterized by scriptural authority (*śāstra*), [they argue that] one who desires to die might engage in intercourse with a woman out of a desire to save her life, thinking, "Let not the life of this poor, high-souled woman be cut short. Such a person does not transgress the prohibition against sexual misconduct. As for the claim that one injunction does not operate within the domain of another, this is not the case; this situation is indeed the domain of the other injunction, because it is characterized by passion.

But surely, even regarding engagement [in action], there is no scriptural injunction, because—unlike in the case of a mandatory rule (*niyoga*)—there is an absence of any traditional rule (*smṛti*) permitting deviation. Now, if it is argued that one engages out of fear of the prohibition—"one might desire killing"—even that prohibition merely forbids violence characterized by passion (*rāga*). And it is not that such a person does not engage out of passion, but rather out of fear of the prohibition. Furthermore, any engagement arising from a desire to benefit others also occurs by avoiding the object of the prohibition. Even if someone were to beg, "I am going to kill myself," and another were to kill him, the latter would not incur the status of a murderer; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the collapse of all worldly conventions (*vyavahāra*). (8.104)
And they should worship Sarasvatī with sacrificial porridges (caru) dedicated to the goddess of speech, effecting the supreme expiation for that sin of falsehood. (8.105)

That which is speech (*vāk*) and is also a deity (*devatā*) is the "speech-deity" (*vāgdevatā*). The *caru* offerings intended for that [deity] are "those having speech as their deity" (*vāgdaivatyāḥ*). *Carus* are rice grains that are not overcooked. Because of the use of the plural number in the injunction "they should sacrifice with them," there is a plural form, *carubhiḥ*. However, this does not mean that there are many individual *carus*, nor does it imply a single sacrifice performed by a collective group, as in the case of the *vrātyastoma* sacrifice, where it is said: "If the god rains, many Brāhmaṇas should sacrifice" (PMS 10.6.45). That is the plural usage; it is not like the rule "and they should sacrifice with three *kapiñjala* birds."

This [statement] is spoken as a falsehood for the sake of favoring Brāhmaṇas and others. "Falsehood" (*anṛta*) refers to the sinful act characterized by the utterance of untruth. Just as with "duty" (*dharma*), the genitive case here is used in apposition. However, according to those who hold that merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are produced by action rather than being the action itself, the phrase "the sin of falsehood" (*anṛtasya yad enaḥ*) involves a non-appositional construction; since the sin has falsehood as its cause, the sin is called "falsehood" through metaphorical usage, even though it is in fact in apposition. Its "expiation" (*niṣkṛtiḥ*) means purification, cleansing, or—synonymously—atonement (*prāyaścitta*). It is "supreme" (*parā*), meaning excellent or pre-eminent.
But surely, how can there be sin here, since it has been stated regarding this occasion that "there is no fault in speaking untruth" (GDh 13.24)?

Some say: "Abstention, however, yields great fruit" (MDh 5.56). However, for one who has made the resolve according to this scripture, "I must not speak an untruth as long as I live," a penance is prescribed so that the fault of a false resolve does not accrue to him. Even regarding the prohibition against arson and homicide, there is a contingent injunction. The phrase "expiation for the sin" (enaso niṣkṛtim) is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*).

How, then, [is it that] they should worship Sarasvatī with offerings dedicated to Speech? If Sarasvatī is the deity of Speech, how is she worshipped? Or, if Speech and Sarasvatī are one and the same, such that there is no distinction between them as deities because the nature of a deity is something to be understood through words, then why are these two terms, "Speech" and "Sarasvatī," distinct? It is just as when one is enjoined, "One should offer to Agni," yet the offering is made with "Svāhā to Kṛśānu, the Flaming One"; or as when it is said, "Having prepared it for Vāyu, one should offer it," even though it is stated, "Vāyu is indeed Breath," one does not offer it saying "To Breath."

True. Speech (*vāk*) alone is the deity. Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) has the sense of a deity. This is because of the use of the accusative case in the word *sarasvatīm*. For a deity is not that which is indicated by the accusative; rather, the accusative denotes the object (*karman*), whereas the deity is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), not the object. How, then, is the word *sarasvatī* to be construed? This is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Just as in the statement, "One offers to Agni; Agni, indeed, is all the deities," so too speech is Sarasvatī. By the sacrifice to her, she too becomes sacrificed to. Through the sacrifice, the deity is understood.

How so? Some say: "Agni is to be sacrificed to; Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to; likewise, one sacrifices to Agni," and so forth. In these cases, the deities are worshipped there and there by their own nature. Here, the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) signifies the worship of a deity, and worship has that which is being worshipped as its object (*karman*). Therefore, the use of the accusative case is appropriate. Accordingly, it is recorded in the Smṛti: "The deity is to be worshipped," and so on.

And this is not tenable; for on this view, the status of being a deity (*devatātva*) would have to be sought elsewhere. In that regard, there is a contradiction with the traditional legal authority (*smṛti*) which states: "The deity is the recipient of the sacrifice. And this *smṛti* is more authoritative because it is independent. The preceding deity is both the object of reference (*uddeśya*) and the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). Since the rule says, "One should meditate in the mind upon that deity for whom the oblation has been taken," the accusative case here is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) of that action. (8.105)
Or he should offer clarified butter into the fire according to the rule with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras,
or with the verse beginning "ud" addressed to Varuṇa, or with the three verses addressed to the Waters.

The mantras called *kūṣmāṇḍas* are recited in the Yajurveda. With them, one should offer clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into the fire. An oblation (*juhoti*) is the relinquishing of a substance with reference to a deity. Since the word "in the fire" (*agnau*) is used here as a locative specification of the locus for the particular pouring (*āghāra*), the deity should be understood as that which is indicated by the wording of the mantra itself. Regarding those mantras in which no specific mark of a deity is seen—for example, in such passages as "Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods" (*devakṛtasyainaso 'vayajanam asi*, VS 8.13)—the ritualists (*yājñikas*) hold that Prajāpati is the deity. Alternatively, it means that whatever deity is seen elsewhere [to be associated with the rite], that is the one connected here. Thus say the authors of the *Nirukta*: "Or rather, that deity may be one chosen at will" (*api vā sā kāmadevatā syāt*, Nir 7.4.5). Even though the deity of one oblation is never the deity of another, nevertheless, the act of sacrificing (*yajati*) is prescribed along with the material and the mantras; therefore, even in the absence of a [specifically named] deity, the form "one should offer" (*juhoti*) must be explained as "one should offer with what follows. But that is incorrect; for in that case, it would have had to be said "one should pour out" (*abhikṣārayet*). We, however, maintain this: in the passage "Thou art the expiation for sin committed against the gods," the very act (*karman*)—namely, the expiation (*avayajana*) or removal—is what is called "expiation" (*avayājana*). Therefore, that [act] is the deity. Furthermore, since there must be some entity denoted by the mantra in every case, there is no absence of the wording of the mantra regarding the deity.

"Either with the verse beginning with *ud*, or with the one addressed to Varuṇa. This refers to the verse beginning with the word *ud*: "O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond from us" (*Ṛgveda* 1.24.15). This verse has Varuṇa as its deity; it is indicated by the opening word *ud*. The specific mention of the verse "addressed to Varuṇa" is for the purpose of excluding another verse that also begins with the word *ud*, namely, "May the hymns exhilarate thee" (*Ṛgveda* 8.64.1). "And with the triplet addressed to the Waters. Here, *daivata* means "deity"; thus, "addressed to the Waters" means that the Waters are the deity of this triplet of verses. It refers to the hymn beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed... (*Ṛgveda* 10.9.1). Consequently, there is one oblation for each individual verse—just like the word "each"—and one collective oblation for the entire set.

The phrase "ghee in the fire" is to be supplied everywhere. "According to rule" means in accordance with the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). Since the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) exists, and since the specific procedure (*itikartavyatā*) has not been previously established, this [verse] authorizes only these much: sweeping around the fire (*parisamūhana*), sprinkling water around it (*paryukṣaṇa*), looking at it (*avekṣaṇa*), the *sruva*-ladle offering (*sruvahoma*), and so forth. Because of the word "or" (*vā*), all of these are indeed optional. (8.106)
If a man who is not ill fails to give testimony regarding a debt or other matters within three fortnights,
he shall be liable for that entire debt and a fine of one-tenth from all his property.

Fifteen days and nights constitute a *pakṣa* (fortnight). The collection of three *pakṣas* is *tripakṣam*. Although the feminine gender would have been expected by the rule "A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in *a* [is feminine]" (*Pāṇini* II.4.30), there is a prohibition because of the observation of forms such as *pātrī* and others. If this is so, then the form *tripakṣī* would not be obtained; however, in that case, there is a Vedic-style transposition of genders. The ablative case is used in the sense of the object when a verbal suffix ending in *-lyap* is elided. The meaning is: he who does not give testimony for as long as three *pakṣas*—even if he is *agadaḥ*, i.e., one whose body is unafflicted—he shall incur that debt. And "a tenth part" (*daśabandham*): a tenth part of that debt shall be imposed as a fine. By the inclusion of the word "debt" (*ṛṇa*) and others in the phrase "in debts and so forth," all legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*) are introduced. The second mention of "debt" is for the purpose of illustration. What is meant is that in whatever legal proceeding testimony is not given for such a length of time, the witnesses of the losing party are the ones who must bear the burden. The word *gada* means disease; it is used here as an illustration for any cause that prevents one from rising to answer. Therefore, in this context, other factors such as family distress or pressure from creditors must also be examined. The word *bandha* refers to a number; in the context of punishment, it denotes ten *māṣas*. The mention of "man" (*nara*) and "from all" (*sarvataḥ*) is for the purpose of completing the meter.

Others, however, say that the meaning of the phrase "he would incur that debt" is this: he would be joined with the sin characterized by the misappropriation of a debt; or, he should pay a tenth part of the fine imposed upon one who has been defeated by the king—thus, having already been punished, he is punished again. (8.107)
If, within seven days of the testimony being given, sickness, fire, or the death of a relative should befall the witness, he shall be compelled to pay the debt and a fine. (8.108)

Regarding the phrase "within seven days," because of the use of the ablative case, the word "before" (*arvāk*) is to be supplied. On any one of the seven days, if a witness is seen to suffer from illness or the like, he is proven a liar by divine means and shall be made to pay [the fine] according to the previously stated rule. Illness that causes extreme suffering, fire that burns cattle or vehicles, and the death of a relative closely connected such as a son or wife—these are the signs of his being a false witness. (8.108)
But in matters concerning which there are no witnesses, when two parties are disputing with one another,
if he cannot ascertain the truth in its true nature, he may cause it to be established even by means of an oath.

Those legal proceedings in which witnesses are non-existent are "without witnesses. In such cases, the king, not knowing the truth, should ascertain it through worldly inference—even by means of the divine inference (daivam anumānam) consisting of an oath, as will be described hereafter. Although the root *labh* signifies "to obtain," it must here be understood as "to know," for there is no other way to "obtain" the truth. This same interpretation applies even if the reading is *na vindan* ("not finding"). The phrase "in those without witnesses, he should ascertain [the truth] by means of an oath" concludes the injunctive statement; the remainder of the verse is merely for the purpose of completing the meter. *Mithaḥ* means "mutually" or "between one another. (8.109)
Great seers and gods have taken oaths for the sake of a particular purpose;
even Vasiṣṭha swore an oath before King Paijavana.

This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the previously mentioned rule of swearing an oath (*śapathavidhi*). For the sake of a legal matter—that is, for the purpose of deciding a doubtful case—oaths were taken by the great seers (*maharṣis*), beginning with the Seven Seers (*saptarṣis*). In this regard, the narrative of the venerable Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana should be cited: when their lotuses (*puṣkara*) had been stolen at Puṣkara, the Seven Seers swore to one another, "He who steals your lotus shall go to this destination of the evildoer," and so forth. [Likewise,] by the gods, beginning with Indra; for Indra, having been falsely accused of [violating] Ahalyā, made various kinds of oaths out of fear of a curse. And Vasiṣṭha—this separate mention is for the purpose of indicating his preeminence. The meaning is that he "performed an oath. Since the specific sense is understood from the prefix itself, the root *śap* (to swear) functions here in the mere sense of "doing. Just as one says "he sacrifices a sacrifice" (*yajñaṃ yajate*) or "he nourishes his own prosperity" (*svapoṣaṃ puṣṭaḥ*), so too should it be understood as "he performed an oath" (*śapathaṃ śepe*). According to the rule "√*śap* in the sense of asserting [something]," the form *śepe* is derived in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), first person, middle voice, singular.

There was once a king named Paijavana. At that time, having been provoked by Viśvāmitra, he entered the sacrificial circle; his conduct agitated by desire and anger, he took an oath, saying, "I am a *yātudhāna*, an *asura*. Viśvāmitra, in the presence of that king, declared: "By this very [act], his hundred sons have been devoured; for he is a *rakṣas*. Then he said: "May I die this very day if I am a *rakṣas*. Here, an oath consists in the invocation of something undesirable upon oneself. This invocation of an undesirable consequence—such as the touching of the heads of one's sons, wife, and so forth—should be understood as an oath. (8.110)
A wise man should not take a false oath even for a trivial matter;
for by taking a false oath, one perishes both in this world and after death. (8.111)

This is the declaration of the consequences for a false oath. "Vṛthā" means otherwise, that is to say, untruthful. In that regard, the fault of a false oath depends on the type of object being stolen, such as gold and so forth; while the fault is slight in a minor false oath, there is certainly a greater fault due to its gravity when the matter at hand is serious. After death, there is destruction in hell; in this world, there is great infamy. Furthermore, if the truth is known through other means of proof, there is punishment by the king. (8.111)
In matters concerning women, marriages, fodder for cattle, fuel, and in providing assistance to Brahmins, there is no sin in taking an oath. (8.112)

*Kāma* is a specific kind of pleasure produced by a particular sensory contact; those women in whom such [pleasure] arises for a man—such as wives, courtesans, and so forth—are called *kāminīs*. In that context, an oath taken for the sake of accomplishing sexual desire, such as "I desire no other woman; you are the mistress of my life," and so on, is permissible. However, regarding the statement, "Let us unite sexually; this must be given by you, and I shall give it," there is indeed a fault in a false oath (*vṛthā-śapatha*). This is a locative of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*), not a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). Therefore, when these [oaths] are made toward a single woman alone, there is no fault in an oath of the aforementioned form. But if it were a locative of cause, there would be a fault in the cause itself—the misappropriation of another's property. Consequently, the prescription of punishment, such as "the former [fine] is tenfold in the case of desire" (MDh 8.121), would not be applicable. Nevertheless, in a dispute arising immediately after the cause, the fault of a false oath certainly exists. This applies everywhere in the same way.

Regarding marriages: "You must not marry another woman, nor should another man marry her"—such a falsehood told for the sake of the marriage of a friend or similar person is not a fault; however, it is not so in cases such as the concealment of caste. Regarding fodder for cows: "I must take this for the sake of providing grass for the cows; I have not taken it"—there is no fault in such a lie told under oath by one who is falsely accused of theft involving another's property or by one who is being sworn falsely. The same applies to firewood. "Providing assistance" (*abhyupapatti*) means favoring Brāhmaṇas.

It is already permitted for the benefit of all social classes (*varṇas*). What, then, is the purpose of this further statement? Some say: "An oath (*śapatha*) is permitted for a Brāhmaṇa, but for Śūdras and others, it is simply a falsehood.

However, because of the statement, "For that [oath] is superior to truth" (MDh 8.104), this is not a falsehood; therefore, there is no prohibition in that case. For that prohibition refers to a frivolous oath (*vṛthā-śapatha*). This is a rule of re-permission (*pratiprasava*) for what was previously prohibited. Therefore, when one swears an oath for the benefit of all classes, there is no fault.

For what purpose, then, is this stated? It is said in response: In that context, protection from execution was prescribed as applicable to all social classes (*varṇa*); however, providing assistance (*abhyupapatti*) is for the Brāhmaṇa alone, for that is possible through the acquisition of wealth and the like. Furthermore, in all such actions involving the property of others, the permission to take an oath should be understood to apply only when success cannot be achieved by any other means. (8.112)
One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons; a Vaiśya, by cattle, seed, and gold; and a Śūdra, by all sins. (8.113)

Now, if one were to cause another to perform an oath consisting of a declaration of action—thinking, "If I were to do this, I would incur this undesirable consequence"—then it is said that he would be swearing. He might say, "I swear by truth," meaning, "May this dharma based on truth and so forth be fruitless for me. In this same way, weapons and vehicles may also serve as instruments; one who swears by them implies, "May these not be fruitless for me. A Vaiśya should swear by touching cows, seeds, and gold with his hand, saying, "May these be fruitless for me," as before. But a Śūdra should be told to swear by all sins: "May the sins about to be described be mine," thus the Śūdra is addressed. (8.113)
One should cause him to carry fire, or immerse him in water;
or else, one should have him touch the heads of his son and wife individually. (8.114)

One should cause him to fetch fire with his hand, shielded by an *aśvattha* leaf; the specific manner of this, such as the distance between the two being seven steps, should be investigated carefully from other *smṛtis*. This very point is stated because it is well-established through tradition. The meaning is that the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) should cause him to immerse himself in water. He should touch the heads of his son and wife—touching the head of the son and the wife with his hand, and also with his speech, since an oath consists of such a form; thus it has been said. [He should do so] separately for each one. (8.114)
He whom a blazing fire does not burn, whom the waters do not cause to float, and who does not quickly meet with misfortune—he should be known as pure in his oath. (8.115)

This heated iron ball, when taken by one who is blameless, does not burn him; nor do the waters cause him to float upward. In an ordeal such as the oath of truth or the *kośa* ordeal, he does not meet with misfortune—that is, he does not suffer pain—as stated in the verse, "Disease is fire" (MDh 8.108). He is pure, clean, and faultless. The limit for this is fourteen days, according to another Smṛti text. 8.115.
For in the past, when Vatsa was falsely accused by his younger brother, the fire—the spy of the world—did not burn even a single hair of his because of his truthfulness. (8.116)

But how is it that fire will not burn and water will not drown? For one might raise the objection: "The great elements do not deviate from their intrinsic nature because they are insentient. Anticipating this inquiry, [the author] confirms the meaning stated by means of an explanatory narrative (*arthavāda*). Even though this matter is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) or is perceptible to the senses, he introduces a Vedic illustration, thinking that [otherwise] it would merely produce a terrifying spectacle like a magician’s trick devised by a rogue, resulting in nothing more than the intimidation of an oath. People become receptive through the acquisition of the meaning, and by seeing what occurred in the past, they attain firm conviction.

There was a seer named Vatsa of the Kaṇva lineage. He was accused and reviled by his younger half-brother, who said, "You are not a brahmin; you are the son of a Śūdra. He replied to him, "By truth I shall enter the fire, if I am not a brahmin. When he had spoken thus and entered, the fire did not burn even a single hair of his. How so? By reason of his truthfulness.

If it is asked how Agni knows the truth, he says: "He is the spy (*spaś*) of the world. One who is hidden in nature and knows what has been done and not done by others is called a spy; he is also well known as a scout (*cāra*) or an informant (*praṇidhi*). For the Lord Agni moves within all beings and is the knower of deeds both done and undone. Thus, there is a usage in the *Chāndogya* and *Tāṇḍaka*: "The gods and asuras were arrayed in battle. Gautama approached Agni and said: 'May your honor move about here as our spy,'" and so forth. Alternatively, even for a specific illustration, the *Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa* should be cited: "Vatsa and Medhātithi were both Kaṇvas. Medhātithi reviled Vatsa, saying: 'You are no Brahmin,' and so on, ending with: 'Not even a hair of his was singed. (PB 14.6.6).
But surely even thieves are not burned, while even virtuous people are seen being burned; so how can there be confidence in an oath?

It is said: This established rule cannot be set aside by observed deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because such deviation is merely occasional. Even in the case of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest, such deviation is indeed observed, yet they are not thereby non-valid. Now, it might be argued that those things which deviate are not even denotable by the term "perception" and so forth, based on the statement: "That which deviates is not perception; that which is perception does not deviate. Here too, one can say the same: "He who deviates is not [the subject of] an oath; that which is an oath does not deviate. But what is an oath? It is that which, having been determined by the mere performance of the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) and so forth, lacks any fraudulent deception or paralysis. Its opposite is a non-oath. For such an oath, there is no deviation. Furthermore, it may be the case that even there, the ripening of the fruit of previously performed karma occurs, since [the oath] serves as the instrumental cause (*nimitta*). One who has committed an offense may be released by virtue of a more weighty merit performed in the past; one who has committed no offense may be punished due to a fault from another birth. For the causes for the manifestation of the ripening of the fruits of karma are diverse. Out of a thousand, perhaps one is falsely apprehended; the general rule (*utsarga*), however, is non-falsity. This is the same even in the case of rites such as the *putreṣṭi* or the *kāmyeṣṭi*.

Therefore, one should believe even in an oath, as if it were given by a witness; for they too sometimes speak falsely. This is not merely a display of fear; oaths are uttered according to their established nature, saying, "May truth prevail. (8.116)
In whatever marriage false testimony has been given, that very transaction shall be annulled; though performed, it shall be as if unperformed. (8.117)

In whatever legal proceeding a case has been decided by means of false witnesses, that proceeding must be set aside; what has been done shall be as if undone. Even if he has received the money, the creditor must be made to restore it, and the other [the debtor], even if he has paid the fine, must be released from it. When it is determined by mere word alone that "you are defeated," it is said that the matter is reversed; the distinction is that this applies even when the proceedings have gone as far as the infliction of punishment. The repetition [of the word] is for the purpose of completing the verse. (8.117)
Through greed, delusion, fear, friendship, desire, and likewise anger, as well as through ignorance and childishness, testimony is spoken falsely. (8.118)

False testimony [is that given] on account of greed and other such motives. The mention of the specific object is for the purpose of determining the particular punishment. "Vitatha" means untrue. In all cases, the ablative case (pañcamī) has the sense of cause. 8.118.
I shall now declare, in due order, the specific punishments for one who gives false testimony in any of these cases. (8.119)

For taking [something] out of greed, one should be fined a thousand; for out of delusion, the first *sāhasa* fine; for out of fear, two middle *sāhasa* fines; and for out of friendship, four times the first *sāhasa*. (8.120)

The construction [of the verse] should be understood as follows: "He who speaks falsely out of greed shall be fined one thousand. In this context, greed (*lobha*) is the cause for one who, having taken wealth from another, speaks contrary to the truth. Regarding "out of delusion" (*mohāt*): this refers to mental confusion (*vaicittya*). One who speaks according to the facts and according to what was seen might, at the time of questioning, be bewildered by some cause of mental agitation; being confused, he might speak otherwise because he fails to grasp the correct meaning of the question due to lack of mindfulness. This is said to be "out of delusion. "Fear" (*bhaya*) means terror. It is the apprehension that if he were defeated by his own truthful testimony, the opponent might perhaps harm him through the loss of relatives, wealth, and so forth. "One thousand" (*sahasram*) is understood as a specific number of *paṇas* from another passage. However, the first type of fine is called "the first *sāhasa*," as in the rule: "two hundred and fifty *paṇas*" (MD 8.138). The phrase "two middle *sāhasas*" is a grammatical modification (*vipariṇāma*). The meaning is that it is four times the previous amount, namely one thousand. Due to the requirements of the meter, that same meaning is expressed through various modes of verbal expression. 8.119–20.
From desire, the former [retribution] is tenfold; from anger, the latter is threefold;
from ignorance, it is two full hundreds; but from childishness, it is indeed one hundred.

*Manmatha* means passion (*kāma*). When women are disputing, if one speaks falsely out of desire for one of them, he shall be fined two hundred and fifty [paṇas]. "Threefold" [of that] due to anger; since the first *sāhasa* (fine) is the subject under discussion, the next higher is the middle [sāhasa]. Or, because it is understood by common worldly usage at the very end, "the highest" itself is the "next. *Dveṣa* means anger. "Out of ignorance" means: if one should state the opposite through delusion, but not at the time of the questioning itself, the fine is two hundred [paṇas]. This refers merely to stating the opposite, not to the act of questioning itself. *Bāliśya* is the state of being a child, i.e., the incapacity for legal transactions (*aprāptavyavahāratā*). This punishment for ignorance applies to one who has slightly passed the stage of childhood but has not yet attained stability of intellect; for any other person, there is simply no status as a witness. 8.121.
The wise have declared these punishments for false testimony to be for the purpose of ensuring that justice does not fail and for the restraint of unrighteousness. (8.122)

He shows that punishment serves both purposes in order to demonstrate its necessity for execution. Dharma is the established order rooted in scripture and custom; its non-deviation is called non-cessation (anivṛtti). 8.122.
A righteous king, having punished them with fines, shall banish members of the three [lower] castes who give false testimony, but he shall exile a Brāhmaṇa. (8.123)

For those who have committed an offense for the first time, the punishment is the former one [as prescribed]. For those who persist in it through repetition, the punishment is banishment from the kingdom—meaning expulsion—or death, as seen in the application of the *Arthaśāstra* and because such is the nature of the rules of punishment. However, a Brāhmaṇa one should exile. "Exile" (*vivāsana*) means the removal of clothing or the destruction of the house. The form [of the word] is derived from the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of "he causes to be without clothes" (*vivāsas*) or "he causes to dwell abroad" (*vivāsa*), with the elision of the suffix according to the rule *ṇāviṣṭavat*. The phrase "the three castes" refers to the three beginning with the Kṣatriya, since a different punishment is ordained for the Brāhmaṇa. (8.123)
Manu, the son of the Self-Existent, has declared ten places for punishment;
when these apply to the three [lower] castes, a Brāhmaṇa should depart unhurt. (8.124)

The word *sthāna* is a synonym for *viṣaya* (object). By these [specified] locations, he who has committed an offense is to be punished. Since the imposition of a monetary fine (*dhanadaṇḍa*) for a Brahmin is prescribed by the term "fine," the instruction regarding his being "uninjured" (*akṣata*) is understood as being for the purpose of avoiding physical injury, even though the number ten is included within the category of wealth.

We, however, say that in the passage, "his entire wealth [is forfeit], yet he remains unhurt" (MDh 8.380), even the infliction of financial penalty is indeed prohibited for a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, for one who has somehow committed an offense only once and is endowed with learning, good character, and noble birth, there is no financial punishment either. And so Gautama, referring to such a Brāhmaṇa, begins with, "In this world, two are firm in their vows" (GDh 8.1), and continues with, "and he is to be exempted from [punishment] by six [grounds]" (GDh 8.12), and so forth. 8.124.
The generative organ, the belly, the tongue, the hands, and the feet as the fifth;
the eyes, the nose, the ears, wealth, and likewise the body. (8.125)

The generative organ is the [part] subject to the law of procreation for both men and women. This is merely a general indication; the specific application will follow later. And where no specific punishment has been mentioned by name, there the offender should be afflicted in that very limb with which he committed the offense. In that regard, for approaching a woman who should not be approached (*agamyā*), there is the suppression of the generative organ. For theft, it is [the cutting off] of the belly by means of the cessation of food and so forth. For verbal and physical violence, it is the tongue and the hands respectively. For one who transgresses by the force of his feet, it is the two feet. For one who, having turned aside, looks lustfully at the king’s wives while they are unsuspecting, it is the eyes. For smelling ointments or perfumes, it is the nose. For listening in secret to the king while he is deliberating, being hidden behind a wall or a curtain, it is the ears. Regarding wealth, the punishment is well known. For the body, the punishment for those who have committed a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*) is execution. (8.125)

Having fully understood the consequences, as well as the place and time in their true nature, and having considered both the strength of the offender and the gravity of the offense, he shall inflict punishment upon those deserving of it. (8.126)

This is the summary verse (*mātṛkā-śloka*) concerning punishments for offenses both specified and unspecified. Following this meaning, the determination of punishment must be made in all cases. In that context, "consequence" (*anubandha*) refers to repeated engagement [in the act] or the cause of such engagement—that by which one is bound to or employed in that action. Having fully understood that: whether it was done out of concern for the hunger of oneself or one's family, or through addiction to religious practices (*dharma-tantra*); or else due to intoxication with liquor, gambling, and the like; likewise, whether through negligence or intentionally, instigated by another, or by one's own will—such is the consequence. "Place" (*deśa*) refers to the village, forest, house, water, place of birth, place of delivery, and so forth. "Time" (*kāla*) refers to night, day, and so forth, or times of plenty or famine, childhood, youth, and so forth. "Strength" (*sāra*) refers to capacity or incapacity, wealth or poverty. "Offense" (*aparādha*) is any one of the eighteen categories. Having examined all of this in its proper sequence, one should inflict or carry out punishment in such a way that the established order of worldly existence (*saṃsārika-sthiti*) is not destroyed. (8.126)
Unjust punishment in this world destroys reputation and ruins fame; it also prevents one from attaining heaven in the next life. Therefore, one should avoid it. 8.127.

Punishment primarily characterized by unrighteousness (adharmapradhānadaṇḍana), or simply unrighteous punishment (adharmadaṇḍana), occurs when one disregards what was previously stated and acts merely on the basis of the literal reading of the scriptures, or by the king’s own whim, or through passion, hatred, and so forth. That [punishment] destroys one's glory and cuts short one's fame. "Glory" (yaśas) is the renown of one's virtues within one's own country; "fame" (kīrti) is that which extends to other countries. Alternatively, "glory" is the reputation for merit while one is alive, whereas "fame" is that which lasts for future times. Fame and glory consist of being faultless and possessing virtues; or another distinction may be inferred, since this is an explanatory statement (arthavāda). It is "not conducive to heaven" (asvargya), meaning it acts as an obstacle to the attainment of heaven produced by other meritorious deeds. The phrase "even in the next world" is for the purpose of completing the verse, since heaven belongs to the hereafter. (8.127)
A king who punishes those who do not deserve punishment, and fails to punish those who do deserve it, incurs great infamy and goes to hell. (8.128)

In the preceding verse, there was a specific rule regarding the determination of the legal consequences (*anubandha*) and so forth; by this [verse], however, the punishment of those who are innocent is prohibited, while its application to those who are guilty is enjoined. Thinking that punishment serves as a means of livelihood, [the king] should not abandon it through excessive leniency. (8.128)
One should first impose the punishment of verbal censure, followed by the punishment of "fie" (reproach).
Third is the punishment of fines, and after that, the punishment of corporal death. (8.129)

If one who possesses good qualities commits a slight offense for the first time, he is rebuked with words: "You have not acted rightly; do not do so again. If, while being thus disciplined, he does not desist, or if he should assert, "What fault is there in this?", then he is censured with harsh words such as "Fie! Fie! and other expressions intended for reproach. If he still does not desist even after that, he should be punished with a fine according to the scriptures. If he disregards even that, he should be struck by means of power and so forth. And the punishment of death consists of beating, amputation of limbs, and the like, but not actual execution itself. (8.129)
As it is said:
"But when one is unable to restrain these [enemies] even by execution, then one should employ all four of these methods against them. (8.130)

If killing is considered execution, what else could there be by which [the offender] can be restrained? And how is this sinner to be suppressed? With such harsh words as these, both fines and execution should be combined for those who are incorrigible. Even if corporal punishment has been inflicted, if he does not desist, then he has not been properly restrained; therefore, one should not let him go, but rather that penalty of execution must be carried out. Furthermore, this undertaking is intended to prevent the recurrence of [offenses punishable by] fines and execution. As for verbal punishment, since it is mild, who would question it? Moreover, execution is seen to be applied again to one previously restrained by a fine, as in the case: "For the cutter of a knot, the fingers [shall be cut off]" (MDh 9.277). 8.130.
I shall explain in their entirety those designations for copper, silver, and gold that are well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transaction.

The designations such as *likṣā* and so forth for copper and other substances are well known in the world; what need is there for technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*) in the treatises? In that regard, their usage by the elders is like that of words such as "cow" (*go*). Therefore, he says: "for the sake of worldly convention. The word "sake" (*artha*) here signifies the object [of the convention]. By this, the established usage in common practice is relied upon.
Consequently, they are well known through usage, being equivalent to words such as "cow"; what is the use of instruction from the treatises?

It is said: this instruction is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). These designations also exist for other measurable things such as iron, bronze, gold, and so forth; therefore, it is intended to exclude them. Furthermore, in some regions there is even a difference regarding the measure of weight, and it is intended to exclude that as well. In some cases, it is restricted by way of its relationship [to a specific number]. Thus, in some places the binding is by forty-eight *māṣas*, in some by sixty-four, and in some by one hundred and eight; all of this is thereby restricted.

And furthermore, the connection is made as follows: "I shall declare those names well-known on earth for the purpose of worldly transaction, so that the entire world may conduct its affairs by means of these alone; otherwise, even the application of punishments and the like would not be established. (8.131)
The subtle particle of dust that is seen when the sun shines through a lattice window is declared to be the *trasareṇu*, the first among all measures of magnitude. (8.132)

Some do not recite this verse, because there is no disagreement regarding the *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust). A *trasareṇu* is that particle of dust which is seen when the sun has entered through the opening of a window-lattice; the word *antara* is a synonym for "opening. First, [the definition] of those measures: || 8.132 ||
Eight *trasareṇu*s should be known as one *likṣā* in terms of measurement;
three of those [make] a *rājasarṣapa*, and three of those [make] a *gaurasarṣapa*. (8.133)

In this context, the measurements are accumulated [as follows]: furthermore, this word *likṣā* does not refer to a tiny sweat-born insect; rather, three *likṣās* constitute one unit of measurement known as a *rājasarṣapa*. It should be applied in this manner. Consequently, those who argue that objects such as barley (*yava*) do not possess the measurements as previously stated are refuted. For there is no fixed measurement for objects such as barley. How then is the meaning of the stated measurement established? It is by way of the designations I shall explain, beginning with "I will declare the measurement. And since the object *trasareṇu* has a fixed measurement, all of this can be determined thereby. Furthermore, skilled persons are able to aggregate *trasareṇus*; thus, this is not an instruction regarding an unestablished entity. This remains an uncontradicted tradition based on the numerical conventions of goldsmiths. Therefore, the actual substance must be precisely and completely ascertained. (8.133)
Six mustard seeds make one medium barleycorn; three barleycorns make one kṛṣṇala;
five kṛṣṇalas make one māṣa; and sixteen of those make one suvarṇa. (8.134)

The word "middle" (*madhyama*) is a cause for non-confusion when it refers to measurement (*parimāṇa*); since [the barley grain] is neither too small nor too large, being the size of a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*), the inclusion of the term "middle" is purposeful. However, if it were intended as a proper name (*saṃjñā*), there would be no point in using the word "middle," because the word "barley" (*yava*) itself functions as the name.

That is incorrect. This composition is not one in which the purpose is stated for each individual member; it is a metrical work (*padyagrantha*). In such a case, even if the meaning is already connected, something is said here in accordance with the requirements of the meter. Furthermore, there is a logical connection (*anvaya*) here. For an expression that lacks connection is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it contradicts the meaning of the sentence. Nor is it [valid] if the expression is not understood. Regarding the various measures (*parimāṇabheda*), such as the *trasareṇu*, the *śatamāna*, and so forth, the specific measure called a *yava* is termed "middle" (*madhya*) because it occupies the middle position relative to those beginning and ending measures.

That which has five *kṛṣṇalas* in it is called *pañcakṛṣṇalikaḥ*. According to the rule “*ata ini-ṭhan-au*,” the suffix *ṭhan* should be applied. In the reading *pañcakṛṣṇalakaḥ*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound ending in the suffix *kap*. Sixteen of those *kṛṣṇalas* constitute one *suvarṇa*. (8.134)
Four *suvarṇas* make one *pala*; ten *palas* make one *dharaṇa*.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together should be known as one silver *māṣaka*.

"Pala" is the designation; "gold" is the designated object. "Four" is the qualifier; "dharaṇa" is the designation; "ten palas" is the designated object. "Two *kṛṣṇalas*" is the designation; they consider "silver *māṣaka*" to be a collective designation. Now, in the instruction regarding the silver *māṣaka*, it is asserted that two *kṛṣṇalas* are to be understood. Consequently, there would be uncertainty. [This is resolved by the following: If they are weighed on a balance-beam (*tulāsūtraka*) that is properly leveled and free from errors of measurement and so forth, the purpose is as with the word "middle" (*madhya*); for if they are weighed without a fixed standard, there would be no certainty regarding the measure. (MDh 8.135)
Sixteen of those silver *dharaṇas* constitute a *purāṇa*; furthermore, a copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is to be known as a *kārṣāpaṇa*, or a *paṇa*. (8.136)

Sixteen silver *māṣakas* constitute a *dharaṇa* of silver; *purāṇa* is another name for it. *Kārṣāpaṇa* and *paṇa* are two names for a copper *karṣa*. Furthermore, the word *karṣa* is taken here as having a meaning well-established in common usage (*loka*), since no deviation [from that usage] is observed; it is not defined by technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) like the term *kṛṣṇala* and so forth. (8.136)
Ten *dharaṇas* are to be known as one *śatamāna* of silver;
a *niṣka* is to be understood by its measure as being equal to four *sauvarṇikas*.

*Śatamāna* is the designation for ten *dharaṇas*. By the word "silver" (*rajata*), gold is also expressed; thus, this is the designation for both silver and gold. However, the measurement of gold is to be determined from another treatise. Accordingly, he will specify later: "But the *śatamāna* is made of silver. (8.137)
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement; five hundred should be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest. 8.138.

In the phrase "middling and highest," the word *sāhasa* (violence/theft) must be supplied. Although the words "middling" (*madhyama*) and "highest" (*uttama*) appear here alone, they are seen in other legal treatises [in connection with *sāhasa*], such as: "By these two, the highest fine for violence is imposed. There, by virtue of the established usage of the treatise and through association, *sāhasa* is understood. The components [of the compound] are clear. 8.138.
When a debt is admitted as due, one deserves a fine of five percent;
if it is denied, that fine shall be double—such is the ordinance of Manu. (8.139)

He who, when brought before the royal court, admits according to the law that a debt is due, saying, "Truly, I owe this to him," deserves a fine of five percent (*pañcakaṃ śatam*); this is the remainder [of the sense]. By this intended rule, one-twentieth part is fined. Why? Because he thinks, "The creditor was sent to my presence; why was he not satisfied right there outside? For this transgression of the scripture, he deserves punishment. But he who commits another transgression and denies it, saying, "I do not owe this to him," when he is subsequently proven by those [witnesses], deserves double that—meaning double the five percent, which is ten percent (*daśakaṃ śatam*). This is the instruction (*anuśāsana*) of Manu Prajāpati, the established order of policy from the time of creation onwards.

Others, however, interpret the word *tat* (that) as referring specifically to what is to be repaid. Thus, "twice that" means twice what is to be given to him. In this way, it forms a single syntactical unit with the phrase "as much as the debt"; otherwise, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Since no specific subject is indicated, if they were to refer to the same subject, an option (*vikalpa*) would result; but that is not appropriate because doubling [the amount] would result in an excessive excess. Even in the absence of an explicit indication, its scope must be shown. Since "five percent" is mentioned in close proximity to it, it is logical that the subsequent reference refers back to that very same thing. (8.139)
One should employ the rate of interest ordained by Vasiṣṭha for the increase of wealth;
a moneylender may take an eightieth part of a hundred per month. (8.140)

“Eighty” is the specification of the rule to be enjoined. “That which was ordained by Vasiṣṭha,” and so forth, is the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Since Vasiṣṭha—the venerable one who knows the three periods of time and is free from defects such as greed—accepted that interest, it is therefore praiseworthy. Wealth increases through it, and there is no defect of greed. One should create [the loan], i.e., one should employ it. When wealth is lent, one should specify that interest at the time of the loan to the debtor. This same measure of interest applies to all goods, such as clothing, grain, gold, and so on. Regarding countable or measurable items, we shall explain later that this is an exception to the rule of doubling [the principal], as in the statement: “The interest on liquids is eightfold” (YDh 2.40). 8.140.
Or he may take two per cent, remembering the duty of the virtuous;
for by taking two per cent, he does not become a sinner through wealth. (8.141)

"Two percent interest is given on this hundred; that is a 'two-hundred' [loan]. This rule of two percent applies to one who previously lent to a person with many dependents. It persists for a month. The passage beginning with "of the virtuous" (*satām*) is here an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). "The duty of the virtuous" (*satāṃ dharmaḥ*): even this interest is the duty of the righteous; by this, their status as righteous persons is not lost. One is not said to be excessively intent on wealth. He shows this: "he does not become a sinner regarding wealth. Sin regarding wealth (*arthakilbiṣa*) arises from seizing the property of others through unjust means; one who possesses that is a "sinner regarding wealth. (8.141)
One may take interest at the rate of two, three, four, five, or ten percent per month, according to the order of the castes. (8.142)

From the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, two and so forth up to four *kalpas* are permitted to be accepted respectively [from each caste]. "Equal" (*samam*) means not more by a quarter (*pāda*) or a half (*ardha*). Even if there is such an excess, because the designation of "two *kalpas*" and so forth does not cease—for instance, it remains "two and a quarter" or "two and a half"—the word "equal" is used to prevent that suspicion; just as even when there is a difference in quantity, it prevents the application of another name. This is also an alternative rule for one who cannot subsist on the former [rate]. Or, this rule applies where one's wealth is small for a great religious purpose and the borrowers are not particularly virtuous, according to the principle: "Those who take wealth from the wicked... (MDh 11.18). There is an alternative reading, "for a year" (*samām*). This interest lasts for one year and no longer; otherwise, because of its magnitude, it would result in doubling [the principal]. (8.142)
But one shall not receive interest on a secured loan if it is used for the debtor's benefit;
nor, due to the lapse of time, can there be a transfer or sale of the pledge. (8.143)

The application [of the pledge] is manifold: it may be taken [as security] or otherwise. The pledge (*ādhi*) is also of two kinds: to be guarded (*gopya*) and to be used (*bhogya*). The pledge to be used is also of two kinds: its use is carried out according to agreement, or it is used in its actual form. An example of a pledge is a milch cow or concealed gold and so forth.

In this regard, the following is stated concerning a pledge that yields profit (*bhogya-ādhi*): "But [this does not apply] when the pledge is productive. Productive means of various kinds: such as a milch cow, a field, a garden, and so forth. While that is being enjoyed—the interest arising from a loan (*kausīdī*), which was mentioned immediately above—one would not receive it; that is, one enjoying the pledge would not obtain any further interest. Even in the case of a pledge for safekeeping (*gopya-ādhi*), if it remains for a long time due to a delay and has doubled in value, yet is not released, there can be neither its transfer (*nisarga*) nor its sale. Transfer (*nisarga*) consists of handing it over according to the prescribed rule to another person. Once transferred to another, even if it has doubled in value, it continues to accrue interest. As he will state later: "Interest is collected once" (MDh 8.151). Sale is well known; that too must not be performed.
What, then, should be done in this situation?

First, one may enjoy the pledge until double the amount of the debt has been recovered. Thereafter, the pledge must be released once double the principal has been entered from the proceeds thereof. (YDh 2.66)

Thus far regarding the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). However, a pledge for enjoyment (*ādhi*) that has yielded its profit remains in place until the pledgor returns. But if the creditor somehow falls into poverty and his remaining wealth is only equal to the amount of the debt, he should wait for some time, report the matter to the king, and sell the pledge. Then, having taken for himself twice as much of his own wealth as was produced from the sale, he should hand over the remainder into the hands of a neutral third party for the sake of the debtor. [Objection: But is it not stated: "The pledge shall be forfeited when the debt has doubled, if he does not release it"? (YDh 2.60)
Thus it is recited.

We shall explain this further below. Because it is subject to destruction (*praṇāśyatva*), there is no loss of ownership for the former owner, nor does the transferor acquire ownership. Furthermore, if giving away (*nisarga*) and selling (*vikraya*) do not exist [in this context], what kind of ownership is said to belong to him? Therefore, by the force of the prohibition, the statement regarding "destruction" is explained as being intended to permit the enjoyment of that which was otherwise prohibited from being enjoyed; or else, it refers to objects such as clothing. For in the case of such things, when they are being used, there is indeed their destruction. Unlike the case of a field or similar property, where ownership remains possible even while the object persists and deviates from its original state, such enjoyability is not possible here. Thus, this should be interpreted according to the established system of the Smṛti.

In this context, "destruction" (*praṇāśa*) and "alienation" (*nisarga*) are used in a figurative sense; however, the prohibition of "sale" (*vikraya*) is used in its primary sense. For that [prohibition] cannot be understood in a figurative sense. Having introduced this very point, another *smṛti* text states: "The two [pledge and mortgage] would not exist if they were dependent on sale. Therefore, here "alienation" (*nisarga*) means "mortgaging" (*ādhyāna*), because of its association with "sale. For those two are similar in certain respects. (8.143)
A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it shall forfeit the interest.
He should satisfy the owner with its value; otherwise, he becomes a thief of the pledge. (8.144)
But has this not already been stated previously: "But never [should he take] a pledge" (MDh 8.143)?

True. Where the interest is exactly equal to the profit, that is the domain of the former rule. However, where the interest is great but the enjoyment is small, if one enjoys [the property] by force or other means, there is a total loss of all interest. In a case where land, cattle, or the like is pledged as collateral, and the enjoyment thereof is not commensurate with the interest—where he does not pay even the accumulated interest, nor has the principal reached double—then, by some exceptional judgment, the interest must be determined to have ceased entirely.

If, however, the garment or other property being used should be destroyed, the user must satisfy the depositor with its value; the latter, moreover, receives the interest. Otherwise, by not returning the value, he would become a thief of the pledge. For the theft of whatever kind of pledge was used, he shall be made to pay the same fine as is prescribed for the seizure of that [property]; "stena" means a thief.

Others explain it thus: there is a loss of interest when one consumes [the pledge] by force; or rather, one should consume it only for its value—that is, the monetary value of the debt. This case concerns one who, while consuming, is told: "Do not destroy my security; do not consume it! I shall release you after a few days. Even though he is told this, if he continues to consume it, that is the subject matter of this rule. (8.144)
Both a pledge and a deposit ought not to suffer the lapse of time;
if they remain for a long duration, both may be forfeited. 8.145

*Ādhi* has its meaning already explained. *Upanidhi*, however, is a deposit placed within a garment and enjoyed out of friendship; whereas a *nyāsa* is a sealed deposit. These two should not be kept for a long time. Rather, they must be released when the proper time arrives. The time for the release of a pledge (*ādhi*) is when the debt has doubled. The transgression of that [time] is failing to release it even at that point. As for a deposit (*upanidhi*), the time for its recovery is as long as there is no occasion for the owner to think, "This is indeed mine; I am the one enjoying it. Any time beyond that is an excess of time (*kālātyaya*). They do not deserve that [excess]; the meaning is that it should not be done. He states the reason: "Those two would become unenforceable. For it is established that if those two remain for a long time and are not recovered, they become unenforceable. Therefore, one should strive to release the pledge when the debt has doubled. This is friendly advice; however, there is no forfeiture of either a pledge or a deposit even after a great length of time, because he will say later: "A pledge, a boundary, and the property of a minor" (MDh 8.149). Thus, this is merely a restatement of that very rule.

Others, however, maintain that this instruction refers to the subject of a pledge (*ādhi*). When someone, out of malice, allows time to pass while the debt has doubled, thinking with such envy: "This wealth shall not increase further by threefold; nor shall he now have the right to pledge or sell it elsewhere; let him not obtain interest here," then it is said in that case: "The two [the pledge and the user] shall be forfeited. By this intention, if he does not release [the pledge], his ownership ceases. But for one who somehow does not release it even when there is no longer any debt, there is neither the right to transfer nor to sell. Alternatively, there is another meaning: he neglects it openly, and it is said with the suspicion that it has fallen into the hands of another: "The two shall be forfeited. (8.145)
When used with mutual affection, these never perish:
a cow, a camel, a draft horse, and a stallion that is being broken in. (8.146)

*Saṃprīti* is simply *prīti* (affection). By means of that [affection] acting as the cause, cows and other such items are enjoyed; they do not perish. Perishing consists in the loss of the former owner's connection and the arising of ownership for the enjoyer; that perishing does not occur in the case of cows and other items being enjoyed through affection. But is it not true that there is no forfeiture of any deposit whatsoever through enjoyment? As he will state: "A deposit, a sealed deposit, and women... (MDh 8.149). What then is the distinction regarding cows and other such items?

It is said: Where there has been possession for ten years and no destruction of the object's essential nature (*svarūpa*), the prohibition regarding a deposit (*upanidhi*) applies to the seizure that would otherwise be obtained through the general rule, "whatever [property]" (MDh 8.147). One might raise the objection that cows and the like do not possess the status of a deposit at all; therefore, this prohibition does not apply to them. However, the word "cow" (*dhenu*) is used here on account of its capacity to conceive (*ādhāna*); if she were to become a cow after a year, and subsequently, having been covered by a bull, were to conceive and thus attain the state of being a cow, then it would give rise to the suspicion: "This belongs to him alone, not to Devadatta. For a four-year-old female in heat (*praṣṭhauhī*) is not something to be enjoyed, whereas a deposit is to be enjoyed with affection. One sees that what is enjoyable is preserved by one's own people and then enjoyed again; however, this is not the nature of a deposit. Indeed, a deposit is meant to be enjoyed. Since enjoyment is absent, how can there be the quality of being a deposit? And yet, this prohibition concerns a deposit. Therefore, since the form of a deposit is transcended, when that prohibition does not apply, another effort is prescribed.

Even in the case of camels and other such animals, after ten years of being used, they undergo a change of state; therefore, in those cases as well, there is no status of a deposit (*upanidhi*). Some consider the term "vahant" (carrying) to be a qualification of the horse. This rule does not apply to a bull (*vṛṣa*). Others, however, consider it to refer to donkeys and mules. A "damya" is a young ox; it is one that is given for the purpose of being employed as a draft animal.

Others, however, consider the negation to have the sense of an alternative: apart from this [stated case], there is another kind of deposit for which there may be an occasional misappropriation. Therefore, in the case of clothing and such items that are used with pleasure, and that which has been worn out, there is indeed misappropriation. For when a garment has been taken with pleasure and subsequently worn out, the owner does not disregard it; nor is there any further opportunity [for him] to say: "Give me back the garment you destroyed; compensate me with its equivalent value. (8.146)
