Whatever property an owner observes being enjoyed by others for ten years while remaining silent and present, he is not entitled to recover it. (8.147)

The phrase “whatever is being enjoyed” (*yat kiṃcid bhujyamānam*) is to be connected with what has been established [in the preceding context]. Although there is a general reference by the term “wealth-owner” (*dhanī*), due to its proximity, it is understood as the neglect of wealth that is being enjoyed. The expression “whatever” (*yat kiṃcid*) includes everything—female and male slaves, raw materials, utensils, and so forth—for these are not universally recognized in the world as “wealth” (*dhana*); rather, it is cows, land, gold, and the like that are more commonly known as highly valuable wealth. Therefore, this is the meaning of the sentence here: if a wealth-owner, the master of the property, observes for ten years whatever substance is being enjoyed by another, yet says nothing, does not bring a legal action before the king, and does not say to the enjoyer in the presence of his family, “This is mine; why are you enjoying it yourself?,” then after those ten years, he is not entitled to recover or claim it. This means that his ownership ceases. By the word “observes,” mere knowledge is expressed, not necessarily direct perception; we shall explain this further under the section on “proximity” (*saṃnidhau*).

By others, not by kinsmen or relatives. And so another Smṛti states: "In the absence of kinsmen and relatives. Furthermore: "If property has been enjoyed by kinsmen, relatives, or those of the same caste, that enjoyment shall not be set aside; one should assume it as a valid enjoyment elsewhere."

That is incorrect; for if that were the case, there would be no fixed rule regarding who are "kinsmen" (*jñāti*) and who are "relatives" (*saṃbandhin*). If one were to grasp merely the fact of a relationship, nothing at all would be excluded. Therefore, it is he by whom another's property is enjoyed who [is considered the owner]. However, if that were so, the word "another" (*para*) would be a mere redundant restatement and thus meaningless, as no one could ever be designated as "another. That [redundancy] is rejected, as in the cases of "husband and wife" or "father and son. For in those instances, the designation applies even to oneself: "The wife is indeed half of one's own self" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 5.2.1.10), and "O son, you are indeed my own self" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 14.9.4.26). Therefore, in the case of husband and wife or father and son, the presence or absence of enjoyment is not the determining factor. Even in their case, when the time for enjoyment arrives, the absence of enjoyment is certainly an obstacle [to ownership], especially when they have divided their wealth. Furthermore, in the case of a wife’s separate property (*strīdhana*), if it has been taken from her by the husband under a legal bond (*bandha*), there is no failure of the husband’s enjoyment; for she is entirely dependent on him. There is no division between the two. Her separate property must also be maintained by him alone. And it is stated in the legal texts: "Excepting the property of the king, a woman, or a *śrotriya*."
Thus, by this [verse], it is stated that there is a loss of ownership for the master who neglects [the property]. 8.147.

The following verse is intended to clarify for whom that [inheritance] is possible; it serves as a supplement to the statement, "he is not entitled to obtain it": "If he is not dull-witted and not a minor... (8.148).

"If he is not dull-witted and not a minor, and his share is enjoyed in the object [of inheritance], then that [share] is forfeited by legal proceedings; the enjoyer is entitled to that wealth. (8.148)

A *jaḍa* is one who lacks understanding. A *pogaṇḍa* is a child; one under sixteen years of age is called a *bāla*, while one over that is called *pogaṇḍa*. This [definition] is intended to indicate other causes for the incapacity to protect one's own property as well. These include: addiction to liquor and gambling, being afflicted by a chronic illness, being solely intent on asceticism and Vedic study, lack of skill in legal transactions, absence of the faculty of speech, and deafness. If these causes of incapacity exist, ownership over the wealth does not accrue to the enjoyer even after a very long time. "In his domain" (*viṣaye*) means that the property of this [owner] is enjoyed. The word "his" (*asya*) refers to the owner. "Domain" (*viṣaya*) refers to Kashmir for the people of Kashmir, and Pañcāla for the people of Pañcāla. Even if the enjoyer and the owner reside in the same region, such a legal proceeding applies to one who is devoid of capacity. Even in this interpretation, this is merely an elaboration, because the mention of "one who is not dull-witted" (*ajaḍa*) and "not a child" (*apogaṇḍa*) has been explained as being for the sake of illustration. Therefore, it should be understood that if a person enjoys another's wealth for ten years, and no cause for such neglect can be conceived by the knowing owner, the enjoyer alone is entitled to it; that wealth becomes his property.

But is it not the case that ownership does not logically arise from possession? It is rather when ownership exists that possession is logical. For if ownership were derived from possession, there would be a lack of settled order. Furthermore, as for this limit of ten years, it is not intended by another Smṛti to apply to all property; rather, it says: "The loss of land belongs to him who sees it being used and remains silent for twenty years" (YDh 2.24). Others, however, do not accept the forfeiture of land even through twenty years of possession, asserting that possession extending over three generations is the authoritative proof (cf. NSm 1.81). Still others, at times, do not admit ownership based on possession devoid of a title of acquisition. For they say thus:
"And he who enjoys [property] without a title, even for many hundreds of years.
Likewise:
"Where possession is observed, but no title is seen anywhere..."
"In that case, tradition (*āgama*) is the cause, not possession; this is the settled rule.
Those who maintain the doctrine of possession by three generations recite as follows:
"That which has been possessed for a long time by three predecessors, even without tradition..."
"That which has come down through three generations cannot be taken away by degrees" (NSm 1.81).

This is its meaning: *āgama* refers to [title] such as a gift and so forth. In the absence of that, what was enjoyed by the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather is established for the fourth [descendant], but not merely by twenty years. Regarding this, it is stated elsewhere:
"In the beginning, the cause is the title; in the middle, possession must be accompanied by title."
But in the case of immovable property, enjoyment alone shall be the sole means of proof.

Success [in establishing ownership] arises from possession for three generations, not from that of the first or second ancestors, the father and grandfather. Even in this case, possession for twenty years is not a valid means of proof. Others, however, maintain that possession lacking a legal title (*āgama*) is invalid even if it has lasted for a hundred years. Thus they say: "But he who enjoys property without a legal title, even for many hundreds of years—the king should punish that sinner with the punishment due to a thief."
But he who asserts enjoyment alone and never the title-deed—there, the title-deed is the cause, not the enjoyment; such is the settled rule. (NSm 1.76*)

As for the phrase "many hundreds of years," this refers to the possessor himself and states his own experience as the reason for the long duration: the meaning is that [ownership] is not established without the possession by one's father and grandfather. But how can there be possession for many hundreds of years by a single person? This is not a fault; words such as "hundred" and "thousand," when used in the plural, are intended to indicate a long period of time. For example: "Man indeed has a lifespan of a hundred years, a hundredfold vigor, and a hundredfold sensory power" (*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 2.17). What is meant is this: ownership is not established merely through possession by the first possessor, even if it exceeds twenty years. Consequently, it is not established for his son either—this is exactly according to the literal text. For it is impossible to remember the original source (*āgama*) over many hundreds of years. And thus, ancient temples of the gods, Brahmin monasteries, and villages might be seized by kings. Even a written edict, being written by a scribe appointed by a king, would not be recognized in its ancient form. Furthermore, the suspicion of a forged edict might arise. Therefore, long-standing possession establishes ownership; it is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the possibility of acquisition through gift-giving and so forth, but it is not the cause (*kāraka*) of ownership itself. For this very reason, possession is listed among the means of proof (*pramāṇa*).

"A written document, witnesses, and possession are declared to be the threefold means of proof" (NSm 1.65). However, this does not refer to [the proofs for] the causes of ownership, such as "the seven ways of acquiring wealth" (MDh 10.115), nor to cases such as "learning, heroism, austerity, and a daughter" (NSm 1.41). Alternatively, this refers to cases where force (*bala*) and the like are suspected to be the cause of possession, as in the passage beginning with "without title" (NSm 1.76*). In this very context, it is stated: "That which is deposited, stolen, entrusted, seized by force, or requested..."
"And that which is eaten [in secret], and these six [other matters]—without [relying on] traditional authority (āgama). (NSm 1.79).
But surely this point is already established by the rule: "A pledge, a boundary... (MDh 8.149)?

No; the meaning of what was stated previously—that one enjoys [the property] for as long as three generations—is the same here. However, this [present rule] is commenced in order to exclude [the right to enjoy it] even after that time. Thus, there is the statement: "for many hundreds of years. "Anvāhitam" means that which is manifest; otherwise, having been shown, it is concealed and something else is substituted. "Hṛtam" means taken at night by means of breaking into a house, deceit, or the like. "Balāvaṣṭabdham" means "forcibly," the word "prasahya" being understood. The rest is well known.

If possession by three generations is the authoritative proof, then what is the meaning of the verse: "The loss of land accrues to one who sees [the encroachment] but does not speak for twenty years"?

Some say: when one has been in possession for such a length of time, even if there are defects in the document—such as its being produced by a capable person through fraud or the like, or due to the omission of sequential syllables—it is declared to be invalid on account of these two [fraud and illegality], and the debtor is thus addressed. Even a document of doubtful form is determined with certainty by this duration of possession.

Others, however, say: where one assigns that very same land as a source of bondage for one person, and that same land for another, such that for the first it is the initial period of validity and for the other it is the subsequent period—there, even though the validity is initial, the twenty-year possession of the latter is stronger.

This, however, is incorrect, because the very person by whom the pledge was accepted is the one who holds it, according to the statement: "The validity [of a pledge] is established through acceptance" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.62). Furthermore, acceptance regarding land is simply the desire for its enjoyment; therefore, in such a case, the establishment of the pledge occurs even after a short period of time. It is with this very intention that it has been said:
"Even though a written document exists, and even though witnesses are living, that which has not been enjoyed—especially in the case of immovable property—is not secure. (Nārada Smṛti 1.68)

The inclusion of the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) implies that there is no lack of proof in the case of cows, horses, and so forth, even when they are not being enjoyed, because those are not necessarily objects of enjoyment. For instance: a cow does not conceive; what kind of enjoyment could she have? Land, however, always yields fruit; therefore, the establishment of ownership (*bandhatva*) cannot occur without the acquisition of enjoyment. Even in that case, if someone who has neglected or abandoned [the property] should have it taken over by a second mortgagee through proximity and so on at the very time of the first enjoyment—while the other [first mortgagee] has not taken possession due to distance from the location or preoccupation with other affairs—then it is considered that ownership is not established by that much alone. However, when one who has indeed taken a mortgage immediately thereafter becomes an ordained monk (*pravrājita*), contracts a severe illness, or has no one else authorized for the protection of wealth and so forth, and he returns after a long time, he certainly obtains his own property even if it has been taken by another, provided that the time for the unconditioned proof [of ownership] has elapsed.

Others, however, say that this [rule] is stated for the purpose of equalizing the redistribution of brothers who have already divided their shares unequally; they maintain that such redistribution does not occur after twenty years. If the result were merely that much, it would have been appropriate to state it in that very context. But its general formulation, by virtue of its elevation from the specific context, indicates that it also applies to other subjects.

Others, however, say: "When a plot of land that has become fallow is brought under cultivation, the enjoyment of that site on the ground is said to have occurred; if the owner has held it for such a number of years, as well as [cultivated it] with plows, fields, and implements, he is the owner of the land and that is the legal domain. [265] Thus they speak.

Now, however, the present-day [authorities] say: "If two persons occupy the same place, possess equal capacity, have the same nature, hold equal wealth, and share common purposes, yet are not related to one another—if one of them, while the other is enjoying [the property], neglects it for such a long duration in their presence, he has no ownership at all over immovable things. Rather, due to the contradiction with the possession by three generations, [ownership] must be entirely denied. For these two Smṛti texts are contradictory; they do not deserve any [forced] interpretation whereby ownership both exists and does not exist, which would be inconsistent. Therefore, this arrangement is logical: although there are many causes for the acquisition of ownership, such as gift, sale, or mortgage, nevertheless, when no specific cause is perceived, it is proper to accept that in the case of twenty-year possession in the matter just shown, it takes the form of a mortgage. Ownership is unstable and subject to enjoyment; if the substance [of the property] diminishes, it may be recovered. Consequently, possession by three generations establishes ownership over everything. As for the suspicion of gift or sale, that will apply only to the annual period. In the case of twenty-year possession, nothing is untenable."

Where both parties proceed by the force of possession alone, without any traditional title (*āgama*), there the prior possession, even if long-standing, is sublated by a present possession of twenty years that is free from defects. It is thus stated that possession for a specific period—characterized by the presence of punishment (*daṇḍapūrvikā*) and occurring during a journey—is a sublater of possession that has descended through three generations.

"It is lost by means of legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*). The mention of "legal proceedings" is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *dharma*. Therefore, if he should somehow know [of the deposit], then he would be defeated. Even then, however, there is no proof for his making known the enjoyment of the deposit; thus, those who engage in legal proceedings are defeated. That is not the rule [for one who knows]; even by such enjoyment, he is ruined. Let this matter rest. (8.148)
A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women, royal property, and the property of one learned in the Vedas do not perish through adverse possession. (8.149)

*Ādhi* is that which is pledged; it refers to a security object such as cattle, land, gold, and so forth, as well as the wealth that is taken from a creditor. *Upanidhi* is described in another treatise as a concealed deposit (*antarhito nyāsaḥ*), which is deposited with its form not shown, covered by cloth or other items bearing marks. However, it is more appropriate to designate *prītibhogya* (that which is enjoyed through friendship) by the term *upanidhi*, since it is already included by the mention of *nikṣepa* (deposit). *Sīmā* means a boundary for villages and the like; because it is common to many, negligence regarding it is possible. For houses and the like, however, there are boundaries consisting of walls, moats, and so forth, or measuring two or three cubits, which are shared by two parties and utilized by one or the other in some way. Because they are small, one might enjoy them and yet neglect them for some time. Even in those cases, one who suspects a cause for the loss of ownership—such as a gift or other transfer—will certainly seize them once their boundaries have been identified by their sons or grandsons through hidden marks and the like. The mention of "the property of a minor" is for the sake of illustration, as the word *pogaṇḍa* has already been shown [in MDh 8.148]. "Women" refers to female slaves or wives. The seizure of other property is not mentioned here, as it is stated [elsewhere]: "For property, the period is ten years" (YDh 2.24).

But surely there is no wealth here; the phrase "whatever" (*yatkiṃcit*) is merely a reference to any object whatsoever. This is not so. By virtue of its connection with the term "wealthy" (*dhanī*) [in MDh 8.47], the general term "whatever" is understood to refer specifically to wealth. Who says that women are not wealth? In this way, the word "wealth" applies to any substance that can be employed [for one's benefit]. Furthermore, from this very fact regarding a woman’s property, ownership in general is indicated. By means of the analogy of wealth, even men are indeed acquired as slaves through enjoyment.

"Royal property": kings are the lords of the land; their wealth is "royal property. For they, on account of their great wealth and high lineage, seek further riches and are consequently destroyed by officials through various means such as false accusations, compared to those who possess less. "The property of a *śrotriya*" refers to the seizure of the wealth of one learned in the Vedas. (8.149)
The foolish man who enjoys a pledge without the permission of its owner must pay half the interest as compensation for that enjoyment. (8.150)

It has been stated: "A pledge must not be used by force; one who uses it [forcibly] shall forfeit the interest" (MDh 8.144). For this refers to the seizure of the entire [pledge]. In that case, when usage is forbidden, one who uses the pledge by force "shall forfeit the interest," meaning he loses all interest indeed. This prohibition applies to what is not permitted. When there is secret enjoyment of the pledge, the pledge is not lost; however, in the case of silver, gold, ornaments, and so forth, the forfeiture of half the interest is declared by this verse.

Regarding new and highly valuable items such as ornaments and clothing that were worn but not lost: it has been explained by the Mahattaras that in such a case, there is not only a loss of interest, but the capital itself is lost and enters [the creditor's possession] after having been squeezed out from its very root. However, Yājñavalkya has explained it thus: where both the owner and the subordinate (adhyadhīna) are involved in the transaction, and a pledge was given by the subordinate and witnessed by the owner, the debtor may at some point ask the subordinate, "I have a need for this pledge. If, having been authorized by him according to the rule of *upanidhi* (a deposit), he uses the pledge at another time, and the owner, seeing it, consumes that authorized pledge—then in such a case, half of the interest is forfeited.

That is incorrect. For the conventional usage regarding master and servant is mutually dependent. In each such case, when one of the two is authorized, this [other] is authorized and employed according to dharma. In such a context, the meaning of the word "master" (svāmin) consists in ownership (*svatva*). Otherwise, he who gives a pledge must necessarily be endowed with mastery (*svāmya*). However, a subordinate (*adhyadhīna*) is not a master. If that were so, then he would be a thief. Therefore, it is a superimposition of mastership. Or rather, in the case of utilization by a subordinate, there is the conventional usage of authorization by the master, as in the case of Brahmadatta. Thus, the previous position alone is correct.

The inclusion of the word *svāmin* (owner/master) is for the purpose of completing the meter. In the phrase *bhuṅkte 'vicakṣaṇaḥ*, the vowel *a* should be understood as being joined by *saṃhitā* [as part of the compound *avicakṣaṇaḥ*]. For he who possesses the thought, "I certainly have interest (*vṛddhi*), as well as additional profit and the enjoyment of goods," is an unwise person (*avicakṣaṇa*). Indeed, there is no rule in worldly or scriptural law that both profit and the enjoyment of goods should constitute interest; therefore, that interest must be enjoyed [as payment]. *Niṣkṛtiḥ* means final purification, which is to say, complete settlement.
Others, however, maintain that this prohibition applies even when the debt has doubled but is still not being repaid, asserting that in such a case the offense is minor.
First of all, they must state the scope of Yājñavalkya’s statement at the very outset: “The pledge shall perish” (YDh 2.60). 8.150.
Interest on a loan, once stipulated, shall not exceed double the principal; for grain, fruit, wool, and beasts of burden, it shall not exceed five times the original amount. (8.151)

Lending money for the sake of profit is *kusīda*; therein lies the interest (*vṛddhi*). Alternatively, *kusīda* is the very wealth belonging to the lender that is being lent out. Money is given with the thought, "Having given a small amount of my own, I shall receive more back"; that is *kusīda*. Regarding it, there is interest. That [interest] does not exceed the point of doubling [the principal]. To that extent—the creditor who has given the money for the sake of interest may receive from the debtor only as much as the principal has entered into a state of being doubled.
But is it not heard that interest becomes double? [In that case] it would amount to three times the principal.

It is not so. A "part" (*guṇa*) is said to be a constituent part; such a part necessarily requires a whole (*avayavin*), and the subject under discussion here is the capital. Therefore, by this method, it is stated that the capital involved in the transaction becomes double. And thus says another Smṛti: "In a long-term loan, there is doubling of the principal" (GDh 12.31), and "The pledge must be released when the debt, having accrued from it, has entered into a state of being double" (YDh 2.66).

Interest is of many forms: when kārṣāpaṇas are lent, interest accrues as kārṣāpaṇas; in some cases it is offspring, as in the rule "or [interest] on women and cattle" (NSm 1.92); and in other cases it is the use of a pledge, such as cows, land, and so forth.

Regarding this, some say that this doubling refers to the case of interest (*vṛddhi*) on items of similar form (*sarūpa*). For in that case, the doubling of interest is understood in its primary sense. However, in the case of a continuous series (*saṃtati*), it is not known whether this doubling refers to the number, or to the measure (*parimāṇa*), or to the weight (*māna*). Thus, there is uncertainty as to which it might be. Indeed, the high value of animals—such as elephants, horses, and so forth—is clearly observed in the context of buying and selling; for those of great size are indeed of high value.

But surely there is indeed similarity within a continuum: the continuum of a cow is simply a cow. In that case, it is not appropriate to propose a distinction such as "growth" and "a similar continuum."

It is said: similarity does not arise merely from belonging to the same genus, but rather from equality in age, size, and so forth. Therefore, the presentation of their distinction is appropriate. As for the attainment of enjoyment (*bhoga*), how is there the perception of doubling? Cows are employed to produce beneficial products; cows, land, and so forth are enjoyed according to their capacity, yielding milk, fodder, and the like. In that case, what kind of doubling is there? Furthermore, such a practice is seen in some places: "Land is enjoyed for hundreds of years until the principal and interest are repaid. And Yājñavalkya recites: "The pledge is enjoyed as long as it has not been returned" (YDh 2.93).

To this it is replied: When only "interest" (*vṛddhi*) is heard, how can it be restricted to the specific case of "doubling"? For a general understanding arising from a scriptural statement (*śruti*) cannot be established in a particular instance without further evidence. As for the objection that doubling is impossible in the case of continuous interest, let effort be made to understand it: when the principal is determined through its repayment, the interest is of the same kind as that from which it arose. Even in the case of the enjoyment of land, such as barley or wheat, equality can indeed be ascertained by means of the value of what is produced therefrom. Furthermore, the word *guṇa* (quality/interest) has the meaning of "benefit. When this is so, how is it understood who possesses equal quality and who is the benefactor? If the interest produced from that [land] is exactly equal to the value produced from the exchange of cattle or grain, then there is equality of quality, even in the absence of equality in quantity and so forth. As for the local custom (*samācāra*) in some places, you yourself have already refuted it by employing the term "in some cases" (*kvacit*). Since the possibility of deviation from custom exists, the *smṛtis* (legal codes) are meaningful as restrictive authorities.

The rule that "the plural is used for many," as in the usage "my eyes are beautiful" (*akṣīṇi me darśanīyāni*) or "my feet are very delicate" (*pādā me sukumāratarāḥ*), is undertaken [in the grammatical treatise]. It is rejected when no such usage is observed. This was stated for the sake of establishing the correct usage regarding the priority and sequence of subordinate elements (*upasarjana*) and prefixes (*upasarga*); for no one, when they ought to say *prapacati*, uses the form *pacati prete*. Even the statement, "The pledge (*ādhi*) is enjoyed only so long as it is not returned," can be interpreted to mean that it continues until twice its value has been paid through the gift. Furthermore, because it forms a syntactical unity with another *smṛti* text, this alone is proper to conclude. And this has been established in detail elsewhere.

"Once established" (*sakṛd āhitā*): by the word "once," it is meant that the application [of interest] has been fixed or accepted as being repeated again and again. "Establishment" (*ādhāna*) is said to mean placing. And determination through verbal arrangement is indeed the same as placing. Furthermore, repeated application occurs when the doubled debt is being taken back. When the creditor, for the sake of doubling the interest, and the debtor, intending to perform a great transaction with that money, effect a renewal of the instrument (*karaṇaparivṛtti*), saying, "The previous interest shall henceforth increase from this day forward," then even though it has already doubled, it continues to increase. Or, if the doubled amount is useful to the creditor upon the transfer to another person, the debtor, being exhorted, hands over another person who will pay, saying, "He will give this to you after so many days"; in that case, the amount being given by his own hand increases again. Nor is this person a surety (*pratibhū*) for the payment, but rather a depositor, the actual giver himself. This, however, has been explained by the straightforward [commentator] as "not transferred to another person" (Bhār on MDh 8.150; p. 113).

Alternatively, even before the doubling [of the debt], when the debtor hands over the pledge to another person—once the coins together with the interest have doubled—the release of that pledge is indeed lawful (*dharmya*). However, while the interest on the pledge remains as it was prior to that day, from that day forward it begins to double again. When the creditor, with the debtor's permission, pledges that same security elsewhere to obtain his own wealth, then the interest increases; this is what is meant by "transferring to another person."

In both cases, once the debt has doubled, the debtor may, by some means, obtain permission from the creditor to take [the loan] from another source; or, if he takes it from this one, the borrower, intending to travel to another region or being occupied with other business, transfers it elsewhere. However, the *Ṛju* (i.e., Bhāruci) does not desire interest exceeding the double amount on that very same debtor when the transaction has not been renewed. Therefore, he says: "When there is no transfer to another person, there is a new transaction. And we shall explain the purpose [of this].

However, as for those who explain: "The interest that has accumulated over a year is all brought in at once; in that case, this rule applies. But where even though it has reached the time for payment, not all of it is given, there one may take more than double"—for them, the word *na* (not) is not used in its literal sense, nor is [the word] *āhita* [used]. For if interest accumulated over a year were to be taken, and there were a further bringing-in [of principal] in the second year, then there would never be a fixed rule of doubling.

Now, as for one who brings back wealth that has doubled along with the profit, let there be a prohibition against anything in excess. Before the doubling [of the principal], he gives only the interest to which he is capable of giving; his taking of the principal is thus not subject to an unlimited amount. This too is of no consequence. It is just that he who carries out the transaction should be favored, not subjected to excessive seizure. However, the claim that one who is somehow recovered by the king even after the debt has doubled should be released from the excess is unjust. Furthermore, this is not the meaning of the word *ahita*.

Now, there is an alternative reading, "āhṛtā" (brought forth). Even so, the word "sakṛt" (once) would not have a certain meaning, and the logical principle (*nyāya*) would be abandoned; furthermore, one's own reading would be established rather than the *Smṛti* of Manu. Thus, the very arrangement [of the text] already stated is what is logical.

In the case of grains and the like, [the interest] does not exceed fivefold—that is, it does not go beyond a fivefold increase. In another Smṛti, a fourfold increase for grain is stated: "The interest on gold, cloth, and grain is twofold, threefold, and fourfold respectively" (NSm 1.92). The settled rule in this regard is as follows: if the lender has become impoverished while the borrower is endowed with great wealth and has used that grain to generate a large profit, then it becomes fivefold; otherwise, it is fourfold. "Sadaṃ" refers to the annual yield, since grain is mentioned separately [from other goods]. "Lava" is well known among the Northerners as referring to wool. "Vāhya" refers to draft animals such as donkeys, camels, oxen, and so forth. (8.151)
An interest rate higher than the established rate, being excessive, is not permitted;
they call that the path of usury, for it allows five percent per month. (8.152)

"Anusāra" (the following) refers to all matters that follow, pursue, and conform to this; it is the conduct prescribed by the scriptures (*śāstra*). This [conduct] is manifold, ranging from the eightieth part [of the principal] up to five hundred percent. Interest exceeding that which has been established such that the debtor cannot satisfy the creditor is [prohibited]. Why? Because it is "excessive," meaning it stands outside the scriptures (*śāstra*).

He states another explanatory passage (arthavāda): "They call that the path of usury. Where base men sink, that is *kuśīda* (usury). By this term, those possessing wealth are characterized according to their conduct. This is a censure meaning: "This is the path, the way, the practice of usurers, not of the virtuous. However, when one must necessarily engage in it—thinking, "This person will accomplish a great task with my wealth"—then, disregarding the distinction of social classes (*varṇa*), he may desire to take five percent per hundred. It is for that purpose that this is stated.

There is an alternative reading: "But that which is made from the essence is superior" [336]. For one who is truly destitute, even if a small amount is made, if he attains great significance through that very wealth or otherwise, that [debt] does not become superior to the person's own worth [337], for it is only that which is worth up to five hundred [paṇas] that is considered supreme. 8.152.
One should not collect interest exceeding that of a year, nor that which is unapproved;
namely, compound interest (cakravṛddhi), periodical interest (kālavṛddhi), stipulated interest (kāritā), and corporeal interest (kāyikā). (8.153)

That which occurs in a year is "sāṃvatsarī" (annual). That which has passed beyond that is "atisāṃvatsarī. The sense of the suffix *bhava* (occurring in) is included by implication. Alternatively, when one reaches the form *atisaṃvatsara* (having passed a year), the two *vṛddhi* augmentations must be applied because of its similarity to Vedic usage.

The interest on those [loans] for which the increase is five percent per month, applicable to all classes of debtors, may be collected for the duration of one year, but not beyond that year. Or rather, [it may be collected] "for as long as a year. A year (*saṃvatsara*) is a full year (*varṣa*). Interest shall not be sought beyond that. Furthermore, after a year has passed, the debtor must not delay [payment].

"He should recover" means he should extract [the debt] from his own property and bring it forward; this is the meaning. Even that which is paid before the end of the year is considered as having exceeded the year.

Alternatively, the increase must be determined by its extent from the month up to the year. The application [of the rule] should be made thus: "that which increases by the month" or "by the year"; however, one who desires the profit for two years does not sometimes cause [the debt] to be held for a long time, thinking, "What is the use of my profit for a few months? If you take it for two years or more, then let this be the interest for such a length of time. Even if he gives it back earlier than that, the debtor should be made to pay the two-year interest as fixed according to the time. Regarding the rule, "One should neither pay nor cause to be paid an interest that is not to be taken," just as monthly interest is made payable when one clears the debt on the very second day of the first month, so too when one agrees that "that which increases by the year" applies, then it is made payable in that same manner, and not as calculated for a period exceeding that.

And one should not collect interest that has not been seen. That which is not seen in the legal treatises—such as the ten-fold or eleven-fold rates, or any rate exceeding the five-fold—should not be accepted. Some maintain that this is a restatement of the rule: "That which is excessive does not succeed" (MDh 8.152). However, this [other interpretation] is more reasonable: "not seen" means "not accumulated. As long as [the interest] has not become consolidated over many months, it should not be accepted; this refers to daily interest or monthly interest. But has it not been stated: "One may take the monthly interest"? (MDh 8.142).
The monthly interest is its [the principal's] increase, but not the taking [of it].

The phrase "he should not even take that" applies by connection to *cakravṛddhi*, *kālavṛddhi*, *kārikā*, and *kāyikā*. "He should not take at all" means this. Although the prohibition is directed against the debtor (*adhamarṇa*), nevertheless, by implication, it should be understood as applying to the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) alone; for what would a distressed debtor not do? Alternatively, "taking away" (*vinirhāra*) is simply "taking" (*grahaṇa*); thus, the prohibition is explicitly stated for the creditor alone.

But surely, since the rules for interest at double and so forth have been prescribed, there is no possibility at all of interest at the "wheel-turning" rate (*cakravṛddhi*) and the like; what then is the purpose of including a prohibition? It is said in reply: A prohibition of what is not otherwise established implies an optional (*pākṣikī*) practice. Just as the rule "one should not sing the *Brahmasāman* at the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*)" indicates by its prohibition that the singing of *Sāman* chants exists even though it was not specifically enjoined, so too these [rates of interest], such as the wheel-turning rate, are permitted by way of their very prohibition. For some who engage in distant trade, even the wheel-turning rate and others do occur. Therefore, it has been said regarding merchants traveling by land and water:
"But those traveling through forests shall pay ten percent; those by sea, twenty percent or one hundred percent;
or they may all, in all types of transactions, pay interest as agreed upon by themselves. (YDh 2.41).

For those traveling through forests and so forth, the interest agreed upon by themselves is common to all castes, but not for others. In that regard, *cakravṛddhi* (compound interest) is defined in another Smṛti: "Interest upon interest is *cakravṛddhi*" (NSm 1.89).

Others, however, define *cakravṛddhi* as interest on vehicles such as carts and the like; this is the increase of that [interest]. For them, interest accrues only on the day the wheel rolls. But when there is no journey due to bad weather and so forth during the crossing of a river, there is no interest. In the same way, for others who employ draft animals such as oxen, such an increase is called *cakravṛddhi*.

Interest based on time (*kālavṛddhi*) is defined as "that which is monthly" (*pratimāsaṃ tu kālikā*; cf. NSm 1.88). The mention of "month" is intended as an illustration. That interest which is not accumulated but is collected day by day or month by month, for which no specific deadline is awaited—namely, that at this time, "if you do not pay, then the debt shall become double"—is of one form: interest based on time.

This is what is meant by *kāritā*. It refers to whatever the creditor and debtor agree upon through mutual consideration of their respective benefits. This rule also applies specifically to merchants traveling in various directions. For others, however, it has been stated that "an agreement exceeding [the interest rate] is not valid," as in the rule: "He deserves five percent per hundred" (MDh 8.152).

Alternatively, when gold is lent and clothes are received as interest, that constitutes *kāritā*, which is a form of collateral (*ādhi*); this would also apply in cases where there is a gain from use or regarding the nature of a deposit (*nyāsa*).
Physical [misconduct] is to be purified by physical action; so too is the livelihood of the body—for those who live by means of camels and the like—in their respective order. (8.153)
He who, being unable to pay the debt, wishes to enter into a new transaction, shall, after paying the interest that has accrued, renew the bond. (8.154)

When a debt has doubled through interest and the debtor is unable to pay it due to the exhaustion of his wealth, he should be made to enter into a new transaction; that is, the instrument—such as a document or witnesses—should be renewed. However, he must pay the interest that has been earned, meaning the amount that results from calculation. This is an exception to the rule stating that more than double the principal shall not be taken. For this is a "new" transaction. Why, then, is it intended as an exception to the rule of doubling? Because there is no such statement here as "the wealth together with interest increases," or "the principal increases. Only a "renewal" (*punar-kriyā*) is heard of. And that has been explained by another interpretation as "he should change the instrument."

If it does not increase, for what purpose then is there a change of the instrument (the creditor)? It is said: when wealth has been acquired through peaceful means and is not being given, there is the possibility of negligence and the like; furthermore, as time passes, witnesses might forget. As it has been said: "In whatever matter one has remained indifferent for ten years..."
In such cases there should be no dispute at all, especially in matters of violence.
Likewise: "A debt neglected for ten years is irrecoverable" (Kautilya Arthaśāstra 3.11.13). And so the ancients used to explain.

And this instruction of the king is a favor toward one who is oppressed. If there is a renewed transaction by way of renewing a doubled debt—where interest is added to the principal plus the interest—that too is a great favor toward the oppressed. Alternatively, if everything is seized at that time but not yet made to be paid, this is a favor for the indigent. Such a favor has indeed been ordained by fate; and thus it is prescribed in all the Smṛtis in such a state:
"Now, if the debtor should be deprived of his capacity due to the lapse of time..."
Having examined his capacity, the debtor should be made to pay the debt at the proper time and place, according to his income.

If the debtor has become impoverished due to misfortune from fate (*daiva*), he must not be oppressed by the king through imprisonment or other such means. What, then, should be done? When he somehow comes to possess wealth, he should be made to pay it back gradually, as far as possible. The phrase "having observed his capacity" (*prekṣya śaktim*) means having ascertained his wealth. He is to be made to pay what is appropriate; for the author will say, "He may also discharge the debt through labor" (MDh 8.177). Therefore, when circumstances have changed, that which we have stated is precisely the intended purpose. (8.154)
Without having shown the gold there, one may exchange it;
one ought to give back as much interest as has accrued. (8.155)

Without producing the gold and without paying the interest-gold due to his poverty, he should have the document renewed right there. In the presence of witnesses, he should say: "I owe him this much principal, and this much interest. He should then record this in the document. They explain that it should be for as much interest as may be possible. Upon renewal, when the principal has been augmented by the interest, a smaller rate of interest must be set—meaning an amount less than what it was before—so that he is not excessively oppressed by the interest.

But according to the opinion of Yājñavalkya, Sahāya, and Nārada, even one capable of paying only a single *kākiṇī* must be made to pay at the time of the exchange of the instrument [of proof]. This is so that the witnesses do not merely possess witness-status through hearing; rather, the debtor’s connection to the object is made manifest before them. For by both hearing and seeing, they will have fulfilled their duty, thinking: "Father, the wealth left neglected for ten years remains in the mind," and thus it will not perish. (8.155)
One who has ascended to the increase of the wheel, being established according to place and time, shall not obtain that fruit if he transgresses the requirements of place and time. (8.156)

"I shall go to Vārāṇasī; let your draft animals and my goods be taken [there], and this shall be your interest. In that case, if he does not reach that place due to a wilderness, crossing a river, civil unrest in the kingdom, or other such obstacles, and returns from an intermediate location with some profit, then the interest as previously determined is not to be paid. For how could there be interest for those who did not reach that destination? For draft animals carrying over a long distance undergo great hardship, and for the owner, the assistance rendered by the draft animals in the form of interest is already accounted for during that time. However, for those who return quickly, the owner indeed achieves further utility elsewhere; this very fact constitutes the transgression.

Thus there is an exceeding of the time limit: "Let my oxen carry [the load] for a month; this much shall be your interest. In that case, if he returns after half a month, the debtor has "ascended to," that is to say, accepted or agreed to, *cakravṛddhi*. Regarding that interest, place and time are fixed—meaning that he has established a specific place or a specific time in the manner previously described, and has not done so without qualification. Such a debtor, by exceeding those [fixed] place and time, shall not obtain—that is, he shall not receive, shall not partake of, and shall not pay—the fruit called interest. (8.156)
Is there no interest at all in that case, or is it five percent? He says: "No.
But whatever interest those skilled in sea-voyages—who perceive the place, the time, and the purpose—establish, that is the basis for recovery in that instance. (8.157)

The mention of "sea-voyage" (*samudrayāna*) is intended as an illustration for any journey in general. Whatever profit land-traders or sea-faring merchants establish is the basis for the determination regarding the acquisition of goods therein; that alone is what must be determined—this is the meaning. This refers to those who perceive and know the prospects of place, time, and purpose, seeing that "in this region there is such an amount of profit," or "in this [time] there is such an amount," rather than those who are merely experts in sea-voyage, such as the helmsmen and others.

Others explain this preceding verse by supplying words according to their own preference (*yadṛcchādhyāhāreṇa*). They argue that when a debtor has agreed upon a specific place and time, and having reached that place, he does not receive the fruit known as "profit" (*lābha*) arising from that location, then what kind of interest (*vṛddhi*) applies there? It is in response to this inquiry that the following verse is given. The mention of "compound interest" (*cakravṛddhi*) is intended to illustrate "stipulated interest" (*kāritā*) as well.

The king should establish as the standard of authority that mutual profit which merchants—who possess an excess of greed—might agree upon, being experts in the methods for managing loss, expenditure, and effort. Regarding the word *tatrādhigamaṃ pratīti*: the prefix *prati* is a *karmapravacanīya* because it denotes the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of attainment (*adhigama*), according to Pāṇini 1.4.90, "In the sense of a characteristic, a state of being so, or a description," and when joined with such [a term], the second case ending is used. (8.157)
If a man stands here as a surety for another's appearance, he shall strive to pay that person's debt from his own property if he fails to produce him. 8.158.

In the lending of money, there are two kinds of security: a surety (*pratibhū*) or a pledge (*ādhi*). Regarding the category of the surety, this is stated: a surety is of three types—of appearance (*darśana*), of confidence (*pratyaya*), and of payment (*dāna*). With reference to the surety for appearance, this is said: "He for whose appearance the surety stands should be shown by me to you in such-and-such a place. Acting thus, he should strive—that is, he should make an effort—from his own means to pay that person's debt; the word "should give" is the implied sense. The mention of "debt" is intended as an illustration for any subject matter of legal dispute (*vyavahāra-vastu*); therefore, whatever matters are enumerated in legal proceedings, the surety, when challenged by one party, must produce that object through his appearance. In cases such as verbal abuse or adultery, a wager (*paṇa*) must be stipulated: "If he is not produced, then I shall pay [the fine]. However, if no such wager has been made, he should be made to pay only the royal fine. But in the case of corporal punishment, the ransom for that is gold. (8.158)
A son is not liable to pay for a guarantee, a frivolous loan, what is due from gambling or liquor, nor the remainder of a fine or a tax. (8.159)

*Prātibhāvya* is the function of a surety (*pratibhū*). That which must be performed by a surety, such as the clearing of another's debt and so forth, is *prātibhāvya*. "Worthiness" (*arhattā*) means fitness; this is what is prohibited here. When that [worthiness] is prohibited, there is a prohibition of entitlement (*adhikāra*). And one who lacks entitlement does not give; thus, it is meant that [the gift] should not be given. In all cases, the verbal form [of the root] *arh* (to be worthy) should be understood as being explained in this manner. But how, then, can a son incur liability for suretyship and the like? Because the father has not taken on that debt.

This is not a fault. Whatever has been accepted as something to be given is indeed equivalent to what has been taken, because its fruit is the same as that of what is taken. Since they have attained a determined nature, they are therefore prohibited.

A "vain promise" (*vṛthādāna*) is a promise made for the sake of jest or similar motives, such as: "Perform this task for me; once it is completed, I shall give you this. When the task has been performed and the father has received [the service], yet the promised gift is not given, the son is not compelled to pay it. This applies similarly to rewards and the like, or matters concerning bards and jesters. Or, for instance, when one says, "I shall cause this merchant to give this much to him," and a messenger is sent, but the payment somehow fails to be made—whether because the merchant was absent or due to some other reason—and the father subsequently dies, the son is not compelled to pay.

*Ākṣika* refers to that which is for the purpose of gambling; it can be understood as whatever is held by a gambler or whatever is borrowed from another for that purpose. This is what is prohibited. That debt which belongs to one who has abandoned his kin and is known to spend his time lying down, sitting, and moving about solely among the gaming pieces—that is determined to be *ākṣika*.

*Saurika* refers to that incurred for the purpose of drinking liquor. The mention of "liquor" (*surā*) is intended to include all intoxicants (*madya*). Therefore, this prohibition applies to the debt of one who is addicted to drinking and is an excessive consumer of intoxicants.

The remainder of fines and taxes: this is a prohibition regarding cases where some portion of the fine and some portion of the tax have been paid by the father, but the full amount of the fine and the full amount of the tax have not been paid.

However, where nothing was given by the father, that [debt] must be paid. It is also stated without distinction in another Smṛti: "The obligations of suretyship, trade, tolls, liquor, gambling, and fines shall not devolve upon the sons" (GDh 12.41). In this regard, there is an option: when the offense is great and the paternal wealth is large, there is a prohibition against the remainder being paid; the same applies to tolls. But when [the debt] is small, the whole must be paid. 8.159.
But in the case of a surety for appearance, the previously mentioned rule shall apply;
if the surety for payment dies, the court shall compel even his heirs to pay. 8.160.

The rule that was enjoined and stated by me in the preceding verse—namely, that sons are not liable for their father’s suretyship in the case of a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhāvya*)—is as follows: if it were so [that they were liable], then the sons of a surety for confidence (*pratyaya-pratibhū*) would have to be made to pay; therefore, he says: when a surety for payment (*dāna-pratibhū*) has died, the heirs, namely the sons, are made to pay, but not in the case of any other [type of surety].

If this is so, then the first half-verse is redundant; for when it is stated that there is no claim against the sons of a surety for payment (*dānapratibhū*), it is understood by implication that there is no such connection with the sons of any other kind of surety. Now, if it is stated for the sake of clarity, the term "surety" (*pratyaya*) must also be included. Otherwise, since the term "seeing" (*darśana*) occurs in the prohibition and the term "payment" (*dāna*) occurs in the injunction, there would be a doubt as to whether the rule applies or the prohibition applies to one who has fallen outside both categories.
There is no doubt, for it has been clearly stated in another Smṛti:

"Where a surety for appearance (*darśana-pratibhū*) or a surety for payment (*prātyayika*) has died, his sons shall not pay the debt; [only those] who stand as sureties for delivery (*dāna*) shall pay. (YDh 2.56)

Here too, because the phrase "as a surety for a gift" is prescriptive in nature, it does not apply elsewhere. The mention of "seeing" (darśana) is for the purpose of illustration; and there is no fault in an illustrative reference within a restatement (anuvāda). If one asks what the purpose is: the composition of the verses by Manu is varied. (8.160)
But when the debtor has not paid, and the surety—whose nature was well known—is dead, by what means may the creditor seek to recover the debt? (8.161)

With this verse, the author, being in doubt, poses a question and resolves it with the answer. The cause of the doubt lies in the two words "adātari" (toward one who does not give) and "vijñātaprakṛtau" (toward one whose nature is known). These words ending in the locative case are explained as being in apposition: "toward one who does not give," "toward a surety," and "toward one whose nature has been ascertained. For what reason would a creditor (*anuttamarṇa*) seek—that is, desire to obtain—the debt? Would he do so through his own efforts alone, or would he also involve the son of that surety? Whence arises the doubt?

It has been stated: "When the deceased is a guarantor for a gift. Therefore, when someone other than him has died, what is the connection to his sons? However, since it is certain that he stood as a guarantor after taking the wealth because his nature was known and the reason was understood, from this there arises the understanding that there is a connection to his sons, because [the debt] was released by him for the sake of clearing that debt.

The word *punaḥ* (again) indicates a distinction from what precedes. If the sons of the surety for payment are connected [to the debt], then when that non-payer has died, the creditor (*dātā*)—that is, the *uttamarṇa*—[may act] after that, meaning at a later time. The rest has been explained. *Parīpsā* is the desire for acquisition. (8.161)
But if the surety has been designated as having sufficient wealth, he shall pay that from his own property; such is the settled rule regarding one who is "designated. (8.162)

*Nirādiṣṭa* means assigned from one's own wealth, entrusted [with the words]: "Become a guarantor (*lagnaka*); this wealth of yours must be settled by you from me if I do not pay. *Alaṃdhana* means possessing sufficient wealth; that is, the full amount of wealth which ought to be given to the creditor has been released. However, if only a small amount has been assigned while a large amount remains to be settled, he should not be made to pay. This is the answer to the preceding question. Even though the guarantor for the payment was not assigned today, his son is made to pay from his own wealth. In the same way, one should understand the term "the son of the assigned [guarantor]" (*nirādiṣṭaputra*), because it is he who is the subject under discussion. If it is argued that the liability of the actual guarantor arises simply from being a guarantor, it is not so. "By means of assignment" (*nirādeśanena*)—this is the established rule, the boundary of the treatise. Since it is already established that the basis [of liability] arises precisely through judicial investigation, the expression "the assigned [son] is the basis" (*nirādiṣṭo 'laṃbana*) is stated in accordance with the requirements of the verse composition. (8.162)

A legal transaction entered into by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted by pain, or dependent; or by a child, or by an elderly person; or one that is not formally concluded, is not valid. (8.163)

The word *vyavahāra* (legal transaction) is a synonym for *kārya* (action). Whatever action there may be—such as giving, mortgaging, selling, and so forth—as well as documents and other means of proof, that which is performed by these [persons] is not established; even though it has been performed, it becomes as if unperformed. "Intoxicated" (*mattonmatta*) refers to those who are well-known to be so. "Afflicted" (*ārta*) refers to one tormented by the loss of wealth, kinsmen, and the like, as well as one beset by imminent fear. Because the words "intoxicated" and so forth are used in their literal sense (*yaugika*), this prohibition indicates the absence of legal validity for as long as they are possessed by intoxication and the like. Furthermore, this is intended merely as an illustration of the state of being "not in one's natural condition" (*aprakṛtistha*). As it has been said:
"Having gone [to another state], one might perform a substitute act;
even that they say is as if unperformed, because he is not independent due to that cause.
And it is said: "One who is not in their natural state is called one whose intellect is overwhelmed, being incapable of discerning their own task. Furthermore:
"Those afflicted by lust and anger, those tormented by pain, fear, or calamity, and those overwhelmed by passion and hatred—these should be known as having fallen from their natural state. (NSm 1.37)

Having formed a *dvandva* compound of *kāma* and the others, [the term] *pīḍita* (afflicted) is used; thus, "afflicted by these" constitutes an instrumental *tatpuruṣa* compound (*sādhana-kṛta*). By this, the exclusion of one who is afflicted is established. Furthermore, such a person is currently under the influence of passion (*manmatha*), desiring the embrace of women and so forth. Those who are "engaged" (*abhiyukta*) are those whose attention is fixed on other activities such as gambling. For these people, being distracted therein, do not attend to the determination of the master's own guarantee (*prātibhāvya*) and so forth—thinking "this belongs to my master"—and thus they are not authoritative. Because their attention is occupied with another activity, when questioned by another, they do not carefully ascertain such things as: "Let this be given to him," "The guarantee was accepted," or "This much of such a thing was stated in this manner. Or, lest there be an obstacle to their current activity, they accept the intention that he remain here, saying, "Go, you; everything you say shall be carried out," thereby accepting a state of dependence (*pāratantrya*). As it has been said: "He is independent because of a cause. That cause by which one who is not independent is not authoritative exists for this person even though he is independent. Just as one who is not independent cannot even employ his own property, so too this person, being overpowered by desire and the like, fails to perceive the distinction between matters or the merits and defects of actions as they are performed, and thus becomes equal to one who is not independent. "Afflicted" (*ārta*) has already been explained. The words *abhiyukta* and *ārta* denote the substratum (*dharmin*), but through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), they should be understood as referring to the qualities (*dharma*). Thus: engagement is "the engaged" (*abhiyukta*); distress is "the afflicted" (*ārta*). "Vices" (*vyasana*) are hunting and so forth, arising from desire and anger. One who is "engaged" (*abhiyukta*) is also called so when performing some activity with intense application, even if not addicted to a vice; likewise, one who is not engaged in a vice may be called so if intent on meditating upon it. Alternatively, the words *kāma* and *krodha* refer to the one who desires and the one who is angry. In this view, the words *bhaya* and *vyasana*, forming a *dvandva* and ending in the third case, are connected with the word *pīḍita*. Others, however, take them as independent terms. "Enveloped" (*parīta*) means pervaded by passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*). Passion (*rāga*) is attachment toward something belonging to oneself; or, regarding someone accepted as one's own, it is the satisfaction of the mind when a desired object related to them is attained. Hatred (*dveṣa*) is the opposite of that, having as its object what is disagreeable. It is the occurrence of satisfaction regarding an enemy who is not one's own, due to the absence of that person's well-being or the contrary. Such are passion and hatred. In every respect, the mental disposition of such a person is unstable and does not remain fixed on the intended task for even a moment. Saying one thing, he does another. One who is of such a nature is "not established in his natural state" (*aprakṛtistha*). Otherwise, all men would be "not established in their natural state" simply because they possess desire and the like, or because they suffer from the ailments of old age, failing eyesight, or headaches. But this is not the case.

The *adhyadhīna*—namely the slave born in the house (*garbhadāsa*), the son, the pupil, and the wife—even though by conventional usage only the *garbhadāsa* is termed *adhyadhīna*, all of these are included here because the term serves as an indicator for those who lack independence. Whatever they do, such as giving away their own property, succeeds only after having obtained the permission of their master. And so says Nārada:
"Whatever act a minor performs, and whatever is done by one who lacks independence, they declare that to be as if not done at all" (NSm 1.35).
A disciple is traditionally considered to be without independent authority, while the teacher possesses independence.
Wives, sons, slaves, and other dependents are likewise without independent authority.
"But that [property] belongs to the householder who possesses independent authority, and it shall belong to him through hereditary succession" (NSm 1.29–30).

Now, if it is said that women lack independence while men possess independence, this is untenable; for wealth is common property. How could a man alone, without the permission of his wife, have the power to give, sell, or otherwise dispose of it?
To this it has been replied:
"Legal transactions entered into by women are declared to be invalid, except in times of distress. (NSm 1.22)

Likewise, beginning with the phrase "the eldest in the family," it is stated: "What he has done shall be considered done; the task is accomplished, not that which was done by one who is not independent" (NSm 1.38). For when wealth is held in common, the man is as much dependent as the woman. Regarding the ownership and dependence mentioned in the word *yat* ("that which"), this appears contradictory; however, it should be understood that ownership exists here, and this is the established rule (*vyavasthā*). Dependence (*pāratantrya*) means being subject to another’s authority and acting in accordance with their will. If one who is dependent does not obtain the power to employ [wealth] without the consent of another, what kind of ownership can he have? Now, regarding giving, pledging, or selling, they lack authority because those acts are the subject under discussion. However, in matters such as the personal use of their own bodies, their own wealth may be employed according to their desire. This applies to twice-born men (*dvija*) who possess great wealth but are dependent and whose selves are restrained by the scriptures, so that they may have personal enjoyment. In the case of a child, both ownership and dependence are appropriate; when he reaches the age of legal capacity (*prāptavyavahāra*), then he shall become the master. The same applies to sons and others. As for a woman, however, there is never a state of non-dependence.
Whether she be a child, a young woman, or even an elderly woman, no action whatsoever should be performed by a woman independently; such is the settled rule. (MDh 5.145)

The inclusion of women within the state of dependence on their masters is stated [here]. By the mention of their dependence, it is not intended to prohibit women from the disposal of their own property. What, then? Transactions such as giving, pledging, or selling are forbidden in inappropriate circumstances. Being dependent, their proper sphere of action must be defined; for they themselves are not capable of discerning such matters—namely, that "this person is a worthy recipient for the acceptance of land, gold, and so forth," "one should enter into a marriage alliance with this man," or "this article is fit to be bought or sold from this person. Therefore, at the time of executing documents and the like, the consent of the husband or other guardians is required. For if the transaction were performed by her alone, there would be occasion for her to say, "I knew nothing of this; I was deceived by you. But when the husband or others have given their consent, what could she possibly say? Thus it has been said.
These authorities also apply if the husband gives his consent;
or, in the absence of the husband, the son; or, in the absence of both husband and son, the king [NSm 1.23].
Thus, even lack of independence has been regulated.
"She is considered to have authority over the disposal and sale [of property], even in cases of intentional misconduct on the part of a child.

(NSm 1.34) The wife and others may be directed by the husband through considerations such as the circumstances of the case, even regarding intentional faults of a child; however, they are not [authorized] to dispose of the husband's property.
"She should be restrained immediately, or she should be abandoned in the presence of the family. (MDh 9.83)

Thus, dependence belongs to women alone and not to men; for even in the case of one who has fallen [from his status], there is an instruction to wait until the completion of his penance. Therefore, there is no sale of slaves and the like, even in some extreme emergency. This is with reference to the statement that "the ownership over them belongs to the master. As for wives, pupils, and female slaves, their dependence is according to their respective roles. However, because wealth is held in common, it is established that a wife has no entitlement to perform sacrifices or other rites anywhere without her husband’s permission. And as for this [text]: "When the husband has died, let the sons remain under her control. (The text here appears corrupt or fragmentary.)
"While both are alive, he shall be dependent, even if he has reached old age;
between those two, the father is superior, and in his absence, the progenitor is considered so"—by this [text], the dependence of sons [is established]; but surely, this is mutually contradictory.

There is no contradiction. A young son who lacks the capacity for authority is dependent upon his mother; however, the mother’s dependence is upon her son. The protection of the mother’s wealth from dangers such as thieves and the like pertains to the son. Furthermore, the son’s dependence upon the father applies only so long as he has not been separated [from the family estate] and continues to reside in the father’s house. But when he has been separated from the father and has acquired wealth by his own effort, then, after the age of sixteen, he should treat his son like a friend;
thus, there is indeed independence.
A child is one who has not yet attained legal capacity, being under sixteen years of age.

An elder is one whose memory has failed, overcome by old age, and past his legal capacity. Even if such a person is at times in his natural state of mind, he is nonetheless not an authority because he lacks reliability. However, in the case of a woman who manages her husband's affairs for the people, an act performed with her authorization is valid.

[455] One who acts without authorization for the sake of another; one who transacts legal business without being appointed—neither a brother nor a father—is not permitted to say, "He owes a hundred [coins] to Devadatta," and so forth. However, in the case of brothers who share a common purpose and all conduct their affairs equally, even if the sale of cattle, goats, and the like, or the pledging of houses and so on, is carried out by any one of them, it is valid because of their relationship. [456] The word *vyavahāra* (legal transaction) is intended to include all types of transactions; however, from the context, it refers specifically to the transaction of debt. 8.163.
A speech does not become true even if it is well-established, if it speaks of phenomena that are external to the fixed conventional [truth]. (8.164)

A word that conveys a certain matter to be performed is generally termed "speech" (*bhāṣā*). Whatever matter is conveyed by such speech is to be performed. Is all speech, then, not true? No, he says: if it is outside of *dharma*—that which is spoken contrary to *dharma*, being opposed to the scriptures and established custom; for example, interest exceeding five percent, the sale of a wife or children, the giving away of one's entire property by an heir, and so forth—even if these matters are established, recorded in writing, or supported by sureties, they do not hold valid. Customary law (*vyāvahārika dharma*) is rooted in practice; it is fixed, beginningless, and not merely modern. This is a continuation of the preceding [topic]: transactions such as gifts made by those who are dependent or not in their natural state of mind are uncertain and thus not authoritative. (8.164)
Whatever is mortgaged or sold through fraud, or given or received through fraud, or wherein one perceives deceit—that the king shall annul in every case. (8.165)

*Yoga* means fraud. When, by means of such fraud, a pledge or the handing over of collateral is made, and it is known that this was done through a false transaction, the King shall annul it. For instance, someone being pressured by a creditor says, "I have nothing. [The creditor replies,] "But you do have a field, a piece of ground, or clothing; hand those over. With this suspicion, the debtor secretly pledges his property to some relative. Then he says, "That has already been made into a pledge by me for another. And this is recognized [as fraud], because even though there is a public document, it is impossible for him to be the pledgor. For if it were truly made as a pledge, how could the pledgor himself continue to enjoy it? Having rendered such a fraudulent pledge invalid, the debtor must be made to give the field and other property to the creditor. Furthermore, when one who possesses ownership through a certain title (*āgama*) at the time of paying the debt creates a different title, that too is a fraudulent pledge. In that case, the debtor—or whoever has had ownership fabricated by this [false] title—must be made to provide the true title.

The same applies to selling and so forth. [471] He who sells a highly valuable object for a small price, or he who does not even take payment from the buyer, or he who says: "This has been sold by me here; this is yours," cannot later say: "This was sold by you to me; take back the price. Furthermore, this rescission of sale (*vikrayānuśaya*) cannot be revoked even after ten days. Or, when there is the previously mentioned cause or another cause, one causes someone trustworthy to buy or sells; yet, in legal proceedings, no purchase with coins and the like is seen to be subject to seizure, nor is there the acquisition through fraudulent sale (*yogavikraya*) based on such grounds as being habitually hoarding coins and the like.

"Yogadānapratigraham" (the giving and receiving of a gift through a connection): when that which belongs to both owners is given after an agreement has been made with one of the parties, namely the recipient, such cases are "yogadānapratigraham. This is a *dvandva* compound formed by analyzing it as "dānaṃ ca pratigrahaś ca" (giving and receiving), treated as a singular unit. Although the mention of either the act of giving or the act of receiving would necessarily imply the other—since otherwise the essential nature [of the offense] could not be established—nevertheless, the mention of both acts is for the sake of completing the meter. Alternatively, if only one act were mentioned, the punishment would apply only to the perpetrator of that act and not to the second party, even though they are an instrument in its accomplishment, because they are not explicitly mentioned by the word. Therefore, they are mentioned separately in order to impose punishment on both the giver and the recipient.
If that were the case, then in the phrase "that which is mortgaged, pledged, or sold," the inclusion of a second action such as "purchase" and so forth would also have to be made.
It need not be made; for even without its inclusion, a penalty would apply based on another Smṛti text or from a general rule.

"Or where one might perceive a pretext (*upadhi*). *Upadhi* means a trick or deception. By this very [rule], a pretext should be excluded from these legal actions even in other cases. For example, someone is told by a creditor: "I will not release you until you provide a guarantor (*pratibhū*) for the payment to be made within such-and-such days. When that person remains silent, someone makes an agreement with the creditor: "Take me as his guarantor while I harass him; he has done me much wrong, and I am a guarantor only for the purpose of harassing him—I shall not have to pay anything myself. Then the creditor says openly: "If you have no other guarantor and do not seek employment or the like, surely you wish to misappropriate his wealth. Being thus harassed, the debtor replies: "I have never had such a transaction with him before. The guarantor then says: "I am your guarantor. Though unwilling, the debtor says, out of fear of harassment and obstruction: "Do as you wish. This [act of the guarantor] is not included among the previously mentioned legal actions.

In this same manner, actions such as agriculture, trade, and the commencement of crafts—those distinct from these [three]—should be illustrated. Giving, mortgaging, and selling are provided merely as examples.

Whatever business is thus effected by means of a contract (yoga), the king shall annul it all. Even if it has been performed, the king shall declare it unperformed and shall not recognize it as valid; he shall punish both the doer and the one who caused it to be done. (8.165)
If the borrower has perished and the expenditure was made for the family, that debt must be paid by the relatives from their own property, even if they are divided. 8.166.

It has been stated that he by whom a debt was contracted must repay it; in his absence, it is to be repaid by his son or grandson; and in their absence, by the one who inherits his estate (*ṛkthagrāhin*). Apart from these, the obligation for another to pay is not intended to apply. Regarding this, in certain specific cases, the following is said for that purpose: if the person by whom the wealth was received has perished, died, or gone to another country—and if expenses have been incurred for the family—then it must be paid by the kinsmen, such as brothers, their sons, paternal uncles, and so forth, even if they are divided and have separate property; the meaning is that each must pay from his own respective wealth. As long as brothers live together, whatever debt arises among them is paid from the household assets themselves; the division of the remainder occurs only after that. As it has been said:

"Whatever debt has been contracted by an undivided paternal uncle or by a brother, or whatever [debt] has been incurred by a mother for the sake of the family, all that they shall pay from the inheritance. [492]

The meaning is that when a debt has been contracted for the sake of the family by any one among those who are undivided, all—the brothers, paternal uncles, their sons, and so forth—must pay it; however, they need not pay a debt not contracted for the sake of the family. Because of the mention of "undivided," such a debt would generally accrue to them alone; for divided persons are never seen taking on debt for the purpose of maintaining another's family. Therefore, he says "even by the divided"; by the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that they must also pay if they are undivided. If, among brothers who are divided, one should go abroad without having provided for the maintenance of his own family, and the other, out of great magnanimity, should maintain that person's family, then even the divided brother or paternal uncle must indeed pay the debt contracted by him when he returns from abroad. (8.166)
Whatever legal transaction a dependent person may carry out for the sake of the family, whether in his own country or abroad, the head of the household shall not annul it. (8.167)

Let brothers and the like be set aside for now. Even a dependent, a household servant, or a domestic worker, for the sake of the family, whatever transaction he may carry out—whether the sale of cattle or livestock, or a loan or a business deal for the purpose of cultivation regarding fields, threshing floors, and so forth, whether in his own country or abroad, while the master of the house is present or absent—that the senior master of the house shall not annul; rather, without further deliberation, he should approve it, saying, "Well done.
Others, however, say that this is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*) supplementary to what precedes, and not an injunction (*vidhi*).

Thus it has been said: "Indeed, there is no seed whatsoever for [interpreting this as] an explanatory statement (arthavāda); for when analyzed, it is expectant [of further completion], because of the connection between the words 'yat' and 'tat' regarding the debt here."

Now, regarding the rule "by one intoxicated, insane, afflicted, or dependent" (MDh 8.163), because a dependent person lacks independence, what he does is not authoritative.
