Furthermore, it is not proper to assume that [an act] is invalid when the master is present for the sake of the family; otherwise, there would be the ruin of the family. Therefore, in an activity consisting of the maintenance of the family, even a dependent person becomes authoritative by force of circumstances. (8.167)
"Whatever is given by force, enjoyed by force, or even recorded by force—all transactions effected by force, Manu has declared to be null and void. (8.168)

Just as that which is done by children, by those who are not independent, by those remaining in their natural state, or by those acting under duress is not authoritative, so too is that which is done by force. The rule is that all matters effected by force are to be set aside; "enjoyed," "given," and "documented" are merely examples. In this context, "given by force" refers to when land, gardens, and the like—which are of no use [to the giver]—are given for the purpose of transport, or when one desiring interest forcibly imposes wealth upon others; or when one forces the carrying of loads upon those who do not wish it; or when one consumes merchandise while depositing the principal value in the houses [of others]. "Documented" refers to the preparation of a written deed. The word "all" means other such matters and transactions as well. Regarding the phrase "a fraudulent mortgage" (MDh 8.165), which was explained there in detail, here too—in this verse—the combination of fraud and force could have been included; however, the two separate verses were composed because Manu’s poetic composition is varied.

"A legal proceeding (*vyavahāra*) is not established when it is brought by one who is intoxicated, insane, afflicted, or dependent; nor when it is done by a child, an elderly person, or by force; nor when it is incoherent or due to a [forced] connection.
Thus, it is simply not established; it does not become valid like a human [judgment]. (8.168)
Three suffer for the sake of others: witnesses, a guarantor, and a family;
whereas four prosper: a Brahmin, a wealthy man, a merchant, and a king.

When another person requests it, testimony, acting as a guarantor (*prātibhāvya*), and overseeing legal proceedings must be performed by the family and others, not by approaching [the task] oneself through force. Therefore, those who act on their own initiative do not become authoritative witnesses. Alternatively, by acting for the sake of another, they incur suffering; for there is not even a scent of self-interest in them. Thus, they should not be made to act by compulsion. "Family" refers to the elder men.

Brahmins and others are honored when requested by another; therefore, a Brahmin should not be made to accept a gift by force against his will. Alternatively, if the accumulation of wealth for the sake of another belongs to the Brahmin, then his activity is for his own benefit and not solely for the sake of another; thus, that Brahmin should not be compelled by force to take or give. The worldly proverb that "giving is accomplished through force" does not prohibit one from making someone give who is unwilling; rather, it means one should make him give if he so desires. However, in the case of a request, there is force.

Thus, one who is wealthy but lives by usury is like a rich man who is not fit for [righteous] purpose. Why? Because he gives his loan to another in business, saying, "Not to me. Or else, if he forcibly causes another—who does not desire it—to incur that expenditure, he must not invest his wealth; for one increases through being requested by others, not by using force, due to the prohibition of the scriptures. In this way, the merchant-usurer conducts business solely with the desire for the increase of wealth. A merchant (*vaṇij*) is one who lives by trade (*paṇya*).

Even a king, when he imposes the royal punishment that has been applied, prospers; but not by conducting legal proceedings through the instigation of forceful persons and the like. As it has been said: "He should not himself initiate a lawsuit" (MDh 8.43). The rule regarding Brahmins and others is a restatement intended as an illustration for the king. Alternatively, this is an elaborate example for everyone, and the same applies to what follows. (8.169)
A king, even when impoverished, should not take what ought not to be taken;
nor should he, even when prosperous, relinquish what ought to be taken, however small the matter may be. (8.170)

Apart from taxes, fines, duties, and so forth prescribed by the scriptures, no other property of the citizens is to be taken by the king, even if his treasury is depleted. However, that wealth which comes through scriptural and legal means as a fee for protection, he must not relinquish, even if it is as small as a single *kārṣāpaṇa*. As it has been said:
"The king should cause his treasury to increase like the path of an anthill. (8.170)
By taking what should not be taken and by rejecting what should be taken, the weakness of the king is made manifest; he perishes both in this world and after death. (8.171)

"Not fit to be seized" means it is not to be taken; [this is expressed by the suffix] *kṛtya* in the sense of fitness (*arhe*), according to Pāṇini 3.3.169. And this has been demonstrated. Weakness is made known by the subjects [with the thought]: "He punishes us, yet he is unable to conquer thieves, forest-dwellers, neighboring kings, and so forth. Thus, the citizens proclaim their own powerlessness toward others. Consequently, when attacked by them, one whose subjects are disaffected perishes in this world, both because of the seizure [of wealth] and because of the unrighteous punishment [meted out] after death. (8.171)
From the enjoyment [of taxes], from the blending of castes, and from the protection of the weak, the strength of a king arises; he prospers both in this world and after death. (8.172)

The non-taking of what belongs to oneself as is rightfully one's due; or rather, "taking" (*ādāna*) here means "taking well" (*śobhanam ādānam*). That which is auspicious (*bhavya*) is indeed "well. The "commingling of phonemes" (*varṇasaṃsarga*) is simply the conjunction of phonemes with those of the same class. Since commingling resides in two things and the two relata are not explicitly mentioned, it is logical that the expectation refers only to the phonemes, as they are the subject under discussion. However, a commingling of phonemes with their intermediate derivatives cannot be designated as a relation belonging to the phonemes alone.

Some, however, read the word *na* (not), [interpreting it as]: "due to the non-mixture of castes. In every respect, this is a restatement of the prohibition against the intermixture of castes. Because of protecting those who are weak and being oppressed by powerful enemies, the king's power is generated. The specific details—that he must conduct legal proceedings correctly and must not inflict unjust punishment—will be recited as explanatory statements (*arthavāda*) for the verses. (8.172)

Therefore, like Yama himself, a master should personally abandon both the pleasant and the unpleasant, and conduct himself with the impartiality of Yama, having conquered anger and subdued the senses. (8.173)

And so he elaborates upon this very point: "This servant is one's own, therefore he is dear; and this other is merely a resident of the kingdom, who remains only as long as the kingdom exists, therefore he is not dear. Having abandoned that [distinction], one should be equal toward all subjects in both protection and legal proceedings. For such is the conduct of Yama observed. Regarding the word 'of Yama' (*yama*), they desire the addition of the suffix *ya* (forming *yāmika*) which supersedes the suffix *aṇ*. But who attains equality with Yama? One who has conquered anger and conquered the senses. One should conquer passion and hatred by means of the abandonment of attachment. (8.173)
But that evil-minded lord of men who, out of delusion, should conduct affairs unjustly, his enemies will soon bring him under their control. (8.174)

He who performs his duties through unrighteousness abandons *dharma* here on earth, utterly deluded by ignorance. This is the fruit born of unrighteousness for him: his enemies bring him under their control because his subjects have become alienated. For when subjects are alienated—being provoked, greedy, fearful, or insulted—they may be incited by others; and then, having brought him under their sway many times over, they punish him, imprison him, slay him, and seize the kingdom. This is what is meant by "bringing under control. (8.174)
But he who, having restrained desire and anger, perceives his interests in accordance with dharma—toward him the subjects turn, as rivers flow toward the ocean. (8.175)

Just as rivers flow toward the ocean and, having reached it, remain devoted to it, becoming one with it and never turning back from it, even so, through the conquest of desire and anger, subjects become one with the king, sharing in his security and prosperity. 8.175.

If one should report to the king that a creditor is recovering his debt by his own will, he shall be compelled by the king to pay a fourth part of that amount as a fine, and the debt itself shall be returned to the creditor. (8.176)

*Chanda* means desire. When, having not obtained the king’s permission, one proceeds by one’s own will through the previously mentioned four means to recover wealth, or when such a person has been summoned by the king’s officers with the words, “I shall detain him in this place; give me the money,” and if, upon being questioned, he admits, “I owe it,” then the king should cause him to pay a fine equal to one-fourth [of the debt]. He should be made to pay the entire debt to the creditor for as much as he owes him. If he owes a hundred, he should be fined twenty-five; a hundred should be made to be paid to him. Likewise in the case of twenty-five. However, one must not fall into this error: that out of a hundred, twenty-five go to the king and the remainder to the creditor. For in that way, the creditor would be the one punished, and not the debtor. (8.176)
A debtor should repay the creditor in equal measure even by means of labor;
one of equal or lower caste may do so, but one of superior caste should pay it gradually. [8.177]

A debtor who is penniless is not released from his obligation simply because of his poverty. What then? He must be made to perform labor. He shall enter into a state of servitude. Whatever amount of wealth a laborer requires to perform that work, that much must be credited to his account even as he works. [548] Labor.

And while he is making payments, if wealth and profit enter [the creditor's hands], there shall be a release from slavery. He should pay equally with the creditor; thereafter, when his wealth is purified, there is no longer the relationship of creditor and debtor. Otherwise, one remains the creditor and the other the debtor, and this state is maintained. A Brāhmaṇa of equal caste is one of the same lineage; one of lower birth is of inferior lineage. One who is superior is of higher caste or possesses greater merit. He should pay gradually, in due order, according to his earnings. It is recited in the *Nārada-smṛti*: "But a Brāhmaṇa, even if impoverished, should pay slowly according to his income" (NSm 2.43). Therefore, for the sake of clearing the creditor’s wealth, the king must not oppress an impoverished Brāhmaṇa, and the creditor must be protected. (8.177)
By this procedure, the king shall bring to a state of impartiality the legal cases of men disputing with one another, which have been established through the testimony of witnesses. 8.178

"By this" is a reference back to the previously mentioned method. "By the rule" means by the prescribed manner. "Established by witnesses and proof": the word *siddha* (established) is to be connected with each term individually; that is, established by witnesses (*sākṣisiddhāni*) and determined by them, as well as by proof (*pratyayasiddhāni*), where *pratyaya* refers to inference or divine ordeal (*daivī kriyā*). "Legal matters" (*kāryāṇi*) refers not only to the non-payment of debts but to other cases as well. "He should bring about equality": he should remove the disagreement between the plaintiff and the defendant and produce a state of consensus.

The non-payment of debts has been concluded; the legal procedure is finished, because in all cases the modes of victory and defeat are of this same nature. Indeed, apart from witnesses and the like, there is nothing else that serves as the basis for establishing the rebuttal in subsequent disputes. Only the specific types of punishment and their nature remain to be stated; thus follows the subsequent elaboration. The nature of "sale by one who is not the owner" and "rescission of sale" is now being established. (8.178)
A wise man should deposit a trust with one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, truthful, possessed of a large following, wealthy, and honorable. (8.179)

One of renowned lineage (*prakhyātābhijana*) is one born of a noble family whose father and grandfather were learned, righteous, and possessed great estates; who, being restrained by their own family traditions, do not engage in improper acts. For such a person is unable to endure even the slightest reproach, and people do not censure him at all. His conduct (*vṛtta*), character (*śīla*), behavior (*ācāra*), and fear of public scandal are innate. "Endowed with" means possessed of these qualities. A knower of Dharma (*dharmajña*) is one who has attained an understanding of its meaning through the study of the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and *Itihāsas*. A speaker of truth (*satyavādī*) is one who, having been observed many times in his affairs, is never suspected of doing something improper when he speaks of his conduct. One with a large following (*mahāpakṣa*)—whose greatness is supported by friends, kinsmen, the king, ministers, and others—cannot be approached by wicked royal officials. A wealthy man (*dhanī*) does not engage in seizing the property of others for the sake of protecting his own wealth or out of fear of the unseen (karmic consequences), thinking: "I have sufficient wealth of my own; what is the use of another's? If it were somehow discovered, I would be punished. A noble man (*ārya*) is one who practices righteousness or is of upright nature. *nikṣepam*: The word *nikṣepa* refers to gold or other goods being deposited; it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object of the action. "A wise man should deposit" means he should place it there for the purpose of protection. By depositing [the property] in this manner, one becomes wise; otherwise, one becomes a fool.

Having become a friend, he instructs [the depositor] regarding what has been seen. This instruction is not for the sake of some unseen purpose, like the *aṣṭakā* rites and the like. When a deposit is placed with such a person, there is no loss; nor does the suspicion arise that it was deposited by someone else with such a person. However, one who is a naked mendicant, a gambler, a drunkard, or the like—even if drawn [to the task] by someone—is not a fit object for suspicion, even if one says, "This was deposited in his hand by my father, and I [received it]," when it concerns a large amount of wealth such as gold; yet this suspicion certainly arises when the matter involves only a small coin (*kākaṇī*). (8.179)
Whatever object a person deposits in another's hand in whatever manner, that must be received back in exactly that same way; as was the delivery, so shall be the receipt. (8.180)

Regarding the word *yathā* (as): in whatever manner [the deposit was made]—whether with a seal (*samudra*) or without a seal (*amudra*), with witnesses (*sasākṣika*) or without witnesses (*asākṣika*), and so forth—it must be received in that very same way. That object deposited must be taken back exactly as it was given or deposited; it is received in the same manner that it was given or deposited. In a case where it is certain that [the depositor] always keeps it in his hand having sealed it, if there is a dispute and the unsealed [deposit] is recovered, and the holder says, "He did not seal it; he took it away from me by force," then in such a case of suspicion, he is defeated. Generally, the sealing is established through other means of proof (*pramāṇa*). However, in another case, if the seal is lost, the King must employ other means of proof to determine the specific quantity of what was stolen. Because of the denial itself, he should be punished with the general fine; but the specific fine for deposit (*nikṣepa*) applies once the quantity of the property has been determined.
But surely, once a total denial has been established, it is only logical that the defendant is defeated.

True. Where the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is established—for example, when Devadatta is accused after a village has been plundered: "On such-and-such a day, that village was robbed by you along with other thieves," and he replies, "I did not go to that village on that day," and the witnesses state, "It was seen on that day; however, that which was stolen there was not seen"—in that case, Devadatta denies the theft as well, because his presence in the village on that day is established. And since another clear cause for his absence is not perceived, it is logical to infer his thievery from his presence at the place and time of the crime. But in this case, the sealed deposit of men who have lost their way through negligence is taken away while still unsealed.

As the delivery was, so was the receipt. With the thought, "What opportunity for my defense is there? a denial may occur; however, one is not able to infer [the truth]. Even if one could somehow cause an inference, the exact amount cannot be established by the testimony of the depositary alone without another means of proof (*pramāṇa*); therefore, a decision based on an ordeal (*divya*) and the like is appropriate. In every case, the determination is that one is "defeated in part" only in that respect where the claim is not possible through another portion. (8.180)
If one who is asked for a deposit does not return it to the depositor, he shall be questioned by the judge in the absence of that depositor. (8.181)

This verse is recited in the traditional collection with its order reversed. Having first recited the first half-verse, one should then recite "in the absence of witnesses" (8.182), and after that, "he is to be entreated. Such a reading is appropriate, for in this way the connection of the meaning is maintained.

This statement is made because ordeals (*divya*) are applicable only when witnesses are absent. Just as in cases such as the non-payment of debts, ordeals are administered immediately after the absence of witnesses, that is not the case here. What then? One should investigate his conduct through spies (*cara*). If, while being investigated with great care, he does not stumble in his behavior anywhere, then he should not be tormented by oaths. But if he falters in this regard, then the suspicion of having misappropriated the deposit is indeed justified; in that case, he must be cleared by means of ordeals. Furthermore, the misappropriation of one deposit does not necessarily prove the misappropriation of another. It may happen that someone, having stolen one item for some weighty purpose, returns it once his need is satisfied, or hands over another item out of remorse. Therefore, this collection of verses is intended to immediately preclude the use of oaths against the holder of the deposit, rather than being a formal presentation of evidence. Nor is it proper to compel the first accuser to pay a fine—even for the unproven theft of another deposit—simply because the judge has been convicted of stealing a deposit. For if one were to be made to pay for an unproven theft simply because of a scriptural rule, then the science of legal procedure (*vyavahāra-śāstra*) would exist merely for the sake of a fixed verdict; and thus, the principle that a verdict must be reached through logical reasons (*hetu*) would be contradicted. Consequently, this matter is neither a scriptural injunction nor a worldly convention. The passage beginning with "in the absence of witnesses" should be understood as having another purpose, according to the manner explained above. (8.181)
In the absence of witnesses, having truly deposited gold with him through spies endowed with youth and beauty, and by means of pretexts; 8.182.

We shall now proceed to the application of the legal principles. That [depositary] should be questioned by the judge (*prāḍvivāka*) in the presence of the depositor. If the depositary denies what was placed in secret by the depositor in his absence while there were no witnesses—saying, "Nothing was deposited by you"—then, once the king has been informed by the depositor, he should not reveal the facial expression of the holder of the deposit. What, then, should he do? He should, through secret agents (*praṇidhi*) or spies, entrust his own gold or silver to another person and have that second deposit requested or demanded by the judge. The mention of the "judge" is intended to indicate any official authorized to reach a decision. Should he request it directly? No; he says it should be done through the mouth of the secret agents. These agents must be endowed with youth and beauty. They should be endowed with youth so that they do not appear as children, for if they were children, others might suspect that their being sent was for the purpose of deceiving me. However, regarding those of mature age, such suspicion does not arise. The same should be explained regarding "beauty": some possess such a form that fickleness appears merely from seeing them. And thus he explains this beauty: "O Blessed One, [grant] freedom from passion. By this, the following is meant: such secret agents should be employed so that the depositary does not suspect, "This undertaking is for the purpose of deceiving me. [He should act] with pretexts (*apadeśa*), with fraudulent reasons for making the deposit, such as royal harassment or going to the village, because stating a reason—"For this cause I am now depositing it with you"—is possible even when false. All of this should be done before the depositor is present. (8.182)
If he should act in accordance with what was entrusted and as it was done, there would be nothing therein for others to bring charges against him. (8.183)

If the holder of the deposit should admit it, saying, "Certainly, it is here; take it," and should deliver it—just as it was deposited: whether sealed or unsealed, as it was originally made, such as cloth and so forth; or if it has been rolled up and remains unsealed, or otherwise, such as an ornament that has not been used and is free from scent, having been placed with the seal of the house or his own mark—if he should return it exactly in that state, there is no truth whatsoever in what others who were previously present allege, namely: "By this man our deposit is denied because of the absence of witnesses. The distinction between "as it was deposited" and "as it was made" is based on whether the marks were hidden or manifest. Alternatively, the distinction is based on the difference in the actions of the receiver and the depositor. "As it was made" means as it was received, without modification and without damage; it must be returned exactly as it was received. The meaning is that in the act of returning it, no lapse of time should be allowed. (8.183)
If, however, he does not pay that gold to them according to the rule, he shall be seized and made to pay both; such is the established law. (8.184)

If those depositors appointed by the judge do not return the deposited property, it is explained by the phrase "according to the rule" (*yathāvidhi*), which refers to the manner in which it was made. That custodian, being restrained by the king’s officers, shall be compelled to pay both—the claimant's due and the king's fine. This is the legal determination of the law; the essential meaning here has been explained. (8.184)
A sealed deposit and an open deposit must never be given to a next-of-kin;
they are lost in his misfortune, but if he does not suffer misfortune, they are not lost. 8.185

Regarding the term *pratyanantara* (next-of-kin): it refers to one who is born immediately after [the depositor], namely the son, brother, or wife of the depositor—whichever has ownership over the property of that depositor. Ownership for the wife has already been stated; likewise for the son regarding ancestral property, and for the brother regarding joint property. In such a case, while the depositor is absent, someone might request from them, "Give us this, for it belongs to us. Thereupon, someone might give it with the thought: "This is common property; one deposited it and another took it away, so what is the harm? Therefore, it is said: "The deposit (*nikṣepa*) and the sealed deposit (*upanidhi*) must not be given to a next-of-kin. He states an explanatory supplement (*arthavāda*) in the form of a reason: "They perish in the event of his misfortune. Misfortune (*vinipāta*) means a change of state for the next-of-kin, such as going to another country and so forth. If that occurs, those two [deposits] are lost [to the claimant]. If he takes it and does not return it to the depositor, then what answer can be given by the holder when questioned by him? To say, "This wealth was taken by your brother, who is a co-owner," is not a valid answer. As it is said: "As the giving, so the taking" (MDh 8.180). To whomsoever it was deposited, whether by the owner or a non-owner, to that very person it must be returned; this verse is an elaboration of that point. However, if the next-of-kin does not undergo such a change of state, then there is no fault even in giving it to him. Thus he says: "But in the absence of misfortune, they are not lost. For in that case, there is an answer: "Do not be angry; therefore I am returning it. The meaning of the verse is that if the next-of-kin has taken it and misfortune has occurred, then one's own wealth must be given to the depositor who requests it. || 8.185 ||
But he who should himself deliver [the deposit] to the next-of-kin of the deceased must not be prosecuted by the king, nor by the relatives of the depositor. (8.186)

Therefore, it has been stated that there is no obligation for the depositary to give back the deposit while the depositor is still alive. However, in the case of one who is dead, if someone gives the property himself without knowing that it belongs to that person, he should not be subjected to the hardship of legal proceedings, such as being made to write documents, on the grounds of whether he knows of anything else or not. One should not trouble him with the thought, "If he had possessed more than this, he would have given that too. Even here, if suspicion does not cease—thinking, "He was very wealthy, yet he did not engage in transactions equal to his means"—then another means of proof must be investigated for the sake of certainty. He should not be tormented by oaths involving poison, fire, and so forth; however, the ordeal of the water-pot (*ghaṭa*), the ordeal of the balance (*kośa*), the ordeal of truth (*satya*), and the ordeal of rice (*taṇḍula*) are not prohibited, for they do not cause excessive suffering. The second rule regarding the absence of witnesses (MDh 8.182) applies here as well; whatever was stated regarding those two rules should be understood to apply here too. (8.186)
He should seek that object with honesty and with affection;
having investigated the man's conduct, he should settle the matter through conciliation alone. (8.187)
In all these cases of deposits, the rule for their recovery shall be as follows:
[the bailee] shall receive nothing from the ocean if he does not recover it from there. (8.188)

Regarding deposits that are being damaged, the procedure just mentioned—beginning with the verse "In the absence of witnesses" (MDh 8.182)—is to be understood as intended for the purpose of resolving the dispute. In the case of a deposit placed in a sealed vessel, the holder of the deposit shall not be subject to questioning by the depositor such as, "There was another substance in this vessel," or "It has been destroyed by worms," and so forth. The same principle should be observed in the case of destruction by rats or similar pests. If clothing or other items were placed in a wooden vessel and the wood were gnawed through and eaten by rats with sharp teeth, there is no fault on the part of the deposit-holder. Furthermore, if a large bundle wrapped in cloth and sealed were deposited, and it could not fit inside the depositor's wooden vessel, then even if it is eaten by rats or others outside, there is indeed no fault. This applies provided that the depositor is aware of this, and the holder has informed him, "I have no other vessel," or if the depositor is someone familiar with the circumstances who might occasionally be nearby. (MDh 8.187–88)
If it has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or consumed by fire, he need not give it back, provided that he does not take anything from that person for himself. (8.189)

If thieves—whether known or unknown—should steal [the goods] by means of breaking through a tunnel or other such methods, the loss falls upon the owner alone, provided that the depositary had taken measures for protection. "Carried away by water" means taken to another region by water. (8.189)
One should investigate the one who misappropriates a deposit and the one who did not entrust it by all possible means and even by Vedic oaths.

One who takes back what was deposited without witnesses, or one who asks for it without having deposited it—or even one who takes it away—should be investigated. Investigation is the effort toward the full ascertainment of the truth through the operation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The "means" are the instruments of knowledge, or alternatively, the methods such as conciliation (*sāma*) and so forth. Therefore, in the case of one whose conduct has lapsed and who does not restore the property, even beating, imprisonment, and the like may be employed—even regarding great wealth—just as in the case of a thief, for the sake of attaining the truth. Punishment is not to be inflicted if the truth is not ascertained. The mention of "Vedic" [deposits] is for the purpose of praise. (8.190)
He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands what he did not deposit—both of these should be punished like thieves, or made to pay a fine equal to the value of the object. (8.191)

This is the punishment for one who denies having deposited [an object] and for one who demands what was never deposited: he shall be fined an amount equal to the wealth regarding which he acts fraudulently. (8.191)

The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value; likewise, he shall do so for the one who misappropriates a sealed deposit (upanidhi), without distinction. 8.192.

The punishment for a thief was stated previously; by that, corporal restraint and the confiscation of his entire wealth were prescribed as optional alternatives for those other than Brāhmaṇas according to their caste distinctions. This [present rule] sets aside that [optionality]. By means of this re-enactment, the punishment for a thief—consisting of verbal censure, fines, and so forth—is combined with the monetary fine, but not the form of limb-mutilation and the like. Furthermore, it is not appropriate to say that the repetition is intended to exclude corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa, since corporal punishment had already been made optional for him by the previous rule; for there is a general prohibition against corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa: "One must never kill a Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 8.380).

A *upanidhi* is that which is used out of friendship; it should not, without distinction, depend upon the nature of the object or its species. Others, however, have defined *upanidhi* in a technical sense, but that [definition] applies only there and not here, because no such technical definition has been provided; therefore, it is proper to accept the word in its ordinary worldly sense. And he will say later: "And of that which is deposited out of friendship" (MDh 8.196). 8.192.
Any man who, by means of fraudulent tests, should seize the property of another, shall be put to death publicly with various modes of execution, together with his accomplices. 8.193.

*Upadhā* means deceit (*vyāja*); *chadma* is a synonym for the same. These are of many kinds. One type is the exchange of goods—such as showing saffron while giving safflower and the like, or the reduction of weights and measures—and so forth. Regarding this, he will state another rule later: "One thing [must not be] mixed with another" (MDh 8.203), etc. Here, however, [the term refers to] intimidation, the display of royal favor, the mention of a maiden's affection, and so on. Having uttered falsehoods such as, "Thieves will rob you if I do not protect you," "The king is extremely angry with you, but I have interceded much on your behalf," "I shall cause the king to grant you the office of city magistrate," "I shall perform a great service for you," or "Puṣpamitra’s daughter is deeply in love with you; she has sent this gift through my hand"—and having thus attached their own gifts, they take back much in return. Then, having secretly reported some other matter to the king or someone equal to him in his presence, they say, "Your business has been commenced," and by such deceptions (*upadhā*) they consume the property of others. For them, this public execution on the royal highway by various means—such as being struck with axes, impalement on stakes, or trampled by elephants—is prescribed.

Others, however, say that this refers specifically to the subject of deposits (*nikṣepa*) within the context; for in that case, one who takes [the deposit] without returning it—thinking, "I deposited it elsewhere, but he is not present and will come tomorrow or the day after"—is a thief. (8.193)

Whatever deposit was made by someone, and of whatever amount, in the presence of witnesses, it must be understood to be exactly that much; one who speaks falsely regarding it deserves punishment. (8.194)

The word *yaḥ* (who) is a designation for the type of object being deposited; *yāvān* (as much as) refers to its quantity. Suppose someone says: "Gold was deposited by me in his hand, yet he gives me bell-metal; and a hundred [coins] were placed with him, yet he gives me only half. He is then asked: "Was this done in secret or in the presence of someone? If he replies: "In the presence of the family (*kula*)," then the family members are the witnesses. When they are questioned therein, whatever they say is the truth. One who speaks falsely—that is, speaks contrarily—is punished. Even in that case, if he should say: "Silver was deposited in the presence of witnesses, but something else was deposited by them without those [witnesses]," then there is occasion here for the operation of other means of proof. This verse also does not intend to establish an additional rule. (8.194)
If a gift was made privately by someone, or accepted privately, it must be returned privately; as the giving was, so must be the taking back. (8.195)

By the rule "in whatever manner one deposits [it]" (MDh 8.180), this procedure for deposits (*nikṣepa*) has been stated; by this same principle, one should proceed in other matters as well. Whether it be the recovery of debts, a sealed deposit (*upanidhi*), a sale, or anything else, it must be returned in exactly the same form and manner in which it was made. That which was done in secret must not be disclosed in the royal court by means of seeking a share of the proceeds or similar tactics. Therefore, when a debt is contracted with a document in one's own hand, the debtor is not compelled to pay a share in the royal court. The wealth of the creditor must be liquidated [by the debtor].

Since this very [rule] already establishes the case of deposit (*nikṣepa*), the repetition there is for the sake of indicating its permanence (*nityārtha*). Consequently, in cases other than a deposit, even if something was done in secret, there may occasionally be a public restitution when there is a suspicion of misconduct. Alternatively, here the disclosure of what was done in private is prohibited; however, in that [other case], the meaning is different—such as "sealed" (*samudra*) versus "unsealed" (*asamudra*)—and thus there is no tautology.

The word *mithas* should be understood as "in secret"; or rather, *mithas* means "mutually. Every transaction, such as giving and so forth, which is to be accomplished by two parties, is performed only between one another. The repetition [of the term] is for the purpose of excluding a third party. The word *dāya* (gift/inheritance) is a general term that denotes not only deposits but also other transactions such as sales and the like. (8.195)
In this manner, the king shall reach a decision regarding both deposited wealth and that which has been entrusted out of friendship, without causing loss to the holder of the deposit. (8.196)

By this, the summary of the section is made. Regarding a deposit (*nyāsa*)—that which is offered out of affection and given for a short time for the purpose of enjoyment—the decision must be made in such a way that the holder of the deposit is not harmed; that is, "without causing injury" (*akṣiṇvan*), meaning without afflicting him. Two or three verses [619] concerning the making of a deposit are intended as injunctions (*vidhi*). Everything else has been established from other sources and is stated here out of friendship [620]. 8.196.
One who sells another's property while not being its owner and without the consent of the owner—one who is a thief yet considers himself no thief—should not be admitted as a witness. (8.197)

This section concerning the legal dispute known as "Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner" is now introduced. If someone who is not the owner—whether it be the son of the owner or another person—sells property or the like belonging to another without the permission of the owner, one should recognize him as a thief or a robber. Even though the one who purchases from him considers him not to be a thief, one should not admit him as a witness. The meaning is that one should not bring that man forward, nor cause him to be brought, nor make him a witness; he must not be appointed for the purpose of giving testimony. For such a person is exactly like a thief; and because of his thievery, he is unfit to be a witness. This prohibition does not apply solely to the office of a witness; rather, it applies to all activities to be performed by virtuous people. Since it is already established that property sold by one who lacks the owner's consent does not become the property of the buyer, this prohibition by way of excluding him from the act of witnessing is intended for the sake of variety. (8.197)

He shall be liable to forfeit [the property] along with his family and pay a fine of six hundred; if he has no connection to it and no means of justification, he shall incur the guilt of a thief. 8.198.

In the preceding section, it was stated that those who perform acts on behalf of others without being the owner—such as acting as witnesses in deeds performed by virtuous persons—are unworthy of the reward. By this [verse], a fine of six hundred is prescribed. "Six hundred" means six hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*; he is to be made to pay—that is, he is to be fined. "Sānvaya" (with kin): *anvaya* refers to a connection through following or relationship. One who has such a person following him—such as a son, a brother, or other relatives of the owner—is "sānvaya. For even if he sells without permission, he is not an obvious thief; for his thought is: "This belongs to me, because it belonged to my father. With respect to him, this suspicion also arises. Having sold it, he pays the price to that very person. However, one who has absolutely no connection is "niranvaya" (without kin). He undoubtedly incurs the guilt of a thief and punishment. "Anapasara" (without a defense): If that house has not been vacated by him, then, being without a defense, he is to be punished like a thief. But if it was given or sold to him from that very house, and because of the owner's ignorance he accepted it or sold it by open purchase, then he is not to be punished like a thief; he is merely to be made to pay the six hundred.

Alternatively, when a relative sells [property], the purchase of that saleable item from another source is *apasara*; an acquisition other than purchase, such as through gift (*pratigraha*) and so forth, is *āgama*. This is what is meant: if he has neither purchased it from anyone nor obtained it through gift or other means, then he is a thief. (8.198)
But a gift or a sale that has been made by one who is not the owner is to be known as invalid; such is the established rule in legal proceedings. (8.199)

It is not only that which is purchased from one who is not the owner that fails to be established; rather, even that which is received as a gift does not succeed. A "gift" (*dāya*) is a donation given through acceptance or out of affection; that too is not established. By the rule, "He sells what belongs to another" (MDh 8.197), the lack of ownership on the part of both the seller and the recipient is stated. This prohibition applies when a claim of ownership might arise based on such rules as "The owner [is he who acquires property] by inheritance, purchase," and so forth (GDh 10.39). This is the settled rule regarding legal transactions (*vyavahāra*), and it must not be transgressed. (8.199)
Where enjoyment is perceived but no scripture is seen anywhere, there the scripture is the cause and not the enjoyment; such is the established rule. (8.200)

In a case where, regarding an object such as cattle, gold, or land, the possession of one person is observed while the title—such as inheritance or gift—which establishes ownership belongs to another, there the title (*āgama*) is stronger than the possession; for possession is merely enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*), which is the cause of ownership. Such is the settled rule. Thus, there is no ownership by mere possession alone, according to the established principle since time immemorial. Furthermore, the nature of that [title] by which ownership is established has been explained previously. Any apparent contradiction with the verse "whatever [property] for ten years... (MDh 8.147) has already been resolved in that very context. (8.200)
